entries.meaning: To be trying to get hold of something, or to be chasing somebody down.
examples: I'm fairly sure she is after my job.
He was after a raise, not a compliment.
Whatever they were after, they didn't find it in the safe.
The marshals have been after him for two years.
The IRS is after my neighbor about a return he never filed.

senses.head: Be trying to get something
body: Used of a thing somebody wants — a job, money, a piece of information. Be stays simple here; the continuous ✗ is being after is impossible. (добиваться, охотиться за)
examples: I'm fairly sure she is after my job.
He was after a raise, not a compliment.
Whatever they were after, they didn't find it in the safe.

senses.head: Be pursuing a person
body: Of police, creditors, or anyone chasing someone down. The person hunted comes straight after the preposition. (преследовать, разыскивать)
examples: The marshals have been after him for two years.
The IRS is after my neighbor about a return he never filed.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ be my job after, ✗ be it after.
entries.verb type: stative — copular be plus a preposition, naming a state of pursuit, not an act. It rejects the progressive: ✗ she is being after my job.
entries.passive: no — be has no passive of its own, so the prepositional passive is impossible: ✗ my job is been after by her, ✗ he was been after by the marshals.
entries.see also: be up to, be on to, be in on

entries.meaning: To arrive — said of a person or a vehicle that is expected shortly. It lives almost entirely in the future: will be along, should be along.
examples: The doctor will be along in a minute.
Wait by the curb — your ride will be along soon.
She said she would be along as soon as the meeting broke up.
Another train will be along in twelve minutes.
Someone from maintenance should be along before noon.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — be along takes no object, so nothing can sit between the two words. ✗ be the doctor along.
entries.verb type: stative in form — the copula plus a particle, so no progressive (✗ the doctor is being along) — though what it reports is an arrival, which is why it lives in the future: will be along, should be along.
entries.passive: no — there is no object, and be cannot be passivized in any case: ✗ she was been along.
entries.see also: be around, be in, blow in

entries.meaning: To be present and available, to have existed for a long time, or — of a person — to have seen enough of life to be hard to fool.
examples: Call if you need help — I will be around all afternoon.
Nobody was around to sign for the package.
That diner has been around since the fifties.
The idea has been around longer than any of us.
He has been around — you won't sell him a story like that.
She has been around long enough to spot a bad contract.

senses.head: Be present, be available
body: The commonest sense, usually about a stretch of time rather than a moment. (быть поблизости, быть рядом)
examples: Call if you need help — I will be around all afternoon.
Nobody was around to sign for the package.

senses.head: Have existed for a long time
body: Of institutions, products, and ideas. Almost always in the perfect. (существовать давно, быть известным)
examples: That diner has been around since the fifties.
The idea has been around longer than any of us.

senses.head: Be experienced, be worldly
body: Informal, and of a person. Said of a woman it can be a slur about her sex life, so Americans use it carefully. (быть тёртым калачом, повидать жизнь)
examples: He has been around — you won't sell him a story like that.
She has been around long enough to spot a bad contract.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: быть поблизости; существовать давно; быть тёртым калачом
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place. ✗ be him around.
entries.verb type: stative in all three senses — presence (I'll be around), long existence (that diner has been around since the fifties), and worldliness (he has been around). None of them takes the progressive: ✗ he is being around.
entries.passive: no — objectless and built on be: ✗ the fifties have been been around since.
entries.see also: be in, be along, be out

entries.meaning: To be depressed, to be out of service, or to be lower or behind in a count.
examples: She has been down since the layoffs.
I was down for a week after the audition.
The whole network is down again.
Payroll was down for six hours yesterday.
We were down fourteen at the half and still won.
Sales are down nine percent from last quarter.

senses.head: Be depressed, be in low spirits
body: Informal, and about mood rather than illness. (быть в подавленном настроении, хандрить)
examples: She has been down since the layoffs.
I was down for a week after the audition.

senses.head: Be out of service
body: Of a network, a server, or a machine — the standard word in American offices. (не работать, лежать — о системе)
examples: The whole network is down again.
Payroll was down for six hours yesterday.

senses.head: Be lower, be behind
body: Of prices, sales, or a score. The amount follows: down nine percent, down fourteen. (снизиться; проигрывать, отставать)
examples: We were down fourteen at the half and still won.
Sales are down nine percent from last quarter.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: быть подавленным; не работать (о системе); проигрывать, снизиться
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place. ✗ be the server down.
entries.verb type: stative — a condition, whether it is mood (she has been down), a dead server (the network is down), or a number (sales are down nine percent). ✗ the network is being down.
entries.passive: no — no object anywhere in the entry, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ the network was been down.
entries.see also: be up, be off, be down with

entries.meaning: To be sick with a particular illness; in slang, to approve of something or be willing to join in.
examples: Half the office is down with the flu.
He was down with strep for most of spring break.
I'm down with that plan.
She said she was down with whatever we decided.
Nobody was down with moving the meeting to seven.

senses.head: Be sick with
body: The illness follows with. This is the ordinary American way to report what somebody has. (слечь с, болеть)
examples: Half the office is down with the flu.
He was down with strep for most of spring break.

senses.head: Approve of, be willing
body: Slang, and dated enough now that it sounds like the nineties. (быть за, одобрять)
examples: I'm down with that plan.
She said she was down with whatever we decided.
Nobody was down with moving the meeting to seven.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the last word, with a lighter beat on down
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ be the flu down with, ✗ be it down with.
entries.verb type: stative — both the illness sense (half the office is down with the flu) and the slang approval sense (I'm down with that) name a state. ✗ he is being down with the flu.
entries.passive: no — be takes no passive, so the object of with stays put: ✗ the flu is been down with by half the office.
entries.see also: be down, be up for, be into

entries.meaning: To be present at home or at work, to be in fashion, to be taking part, or — of results and arrivals — to have come in.
examples: Is Dr. Alvarez in today?
Nobody was in when the inspector came by.
Wide lapels are in again.
Flip phones were in long before anyone called them retro.
If you're putting a team together, I'm in.
He was in until he saw the budget.
The flight is in early.
The lab results are in, and they're clean.

senses.head: Be present, be at home or at the office
body: Of a person others are looking for. (быть на месте, быть дома)
examples: Is Dr. Alvarez in today?
Nobody was in when the inspector came by.

senses.head: Be in fashion
body: The opposite of be out. (быть в моде)
examples: Wide lapels are in again.
Flip phones were in long before anyone called them retro.

senses.head: Be taking part, be included
body: Usually the short answer I'm in. (участвовать, быть в деле)
examples: If you're putting a team together, I'm in.
He was in until he saw the budget.

senses.head: Have arrived, have come in
body: Of flights, harvests, votes, and lab results. (прибыть; поступить — о результатах)
examples: The flight is in early.
The lab results are in, and they're clean.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: быть на месте; быть в моде; участвовать; поступить (о результатах)
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place. ✗ be the doctor in as a statement; the question Is the doctor in? is ordinary inversion, not separation.
entries.verb type: stative — presence (the doctor is in), fashion (wide lapels are in), participation (I'm in), and arrival of results (the votes are in) are all states. ✗ the doctor is being in.
entries.passive: no — intransitive throughout, and the copula has no passive: ✗ the votes were been in.
entries.see also: be out, be around, be in on

entries.meaning: To be about to experience something, almost always something unpleasant.
examples: If he thinks that drive is easy, he is in for a surprise.
We are in for a rough winter.
She was in for a long wait at the DMV.
Anyone who skipped the reading is in for trouble tomorrow.
They didn't know they were in for three more hours of delays.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on in; for is reduced to a schwa
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ be a surprise in for, ✗ be it in for.
entries.verb type: stative — it reports what is in store for someone, not anything the subject does: we are in for a rough winter. ✗ we are being in for a rough winter.
entries.passive: no — the object of for cannot move to subject: ✗ a surprise is been in for by him.
entries.see also: be up for, be in, be out of

entries.meaning: To be one of the people who know about or take part in something, usually something private.
examples: Only three people were in on the surprise.
Was the manager in on it, or did he really not know?
I want to be in on the next round of hiring.
Everybody at that table was in on the joke but me.
She has been in on the planning since the first week.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on in, the first of the two particles
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ be the joke in on, ✗ be it in on.
entries.verb type: stative — being one of the people who know or take part is a standing condition: she has been in on the planning since the first week. ✗ she is being in on it.
entries.passive: no — built on be, so no passive at all: ✗ the joke was been in on by everybody.
entries.see also: be in, be up to, be on to

entries.meaning: To be keenly interested in something, or attracted to someone.
examples: He is into vintage synthesizers.
She was into rock climbing long before the gyms opened.
I'm not into podcasts about podcasts.
I don't think she is into me.
They dated for a month before he admitted he wasn't into it.

senses.head: Be keen on an activity or subject
body: The everyday way an American says what a hobby is. (увлекаться, интересоваться)
examples: He is into vintage synthesizers.
She was into rock climbing long before the gyms opened.
I'm not into podcasts about podcasts.

senses.head: Be attracted to a person
body: Of romantic interest, and usually negative. (быть неравнодушным к, нравиться)
examples: I don't think she is into me.
They dated for a month before he admitted he wasn't into it.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition: he is into synthesizers, never ✗ he is synthesizers into; with a pronoun, she is into it, never ✗ she is it into.
entries.verb type: stative — a state of interest or attraction, whether the object is a hobby (he is into synthesizers) or a person (she is into him). ✗ he is being into synthesizers.
entries.passive: no — ✗ synthesizers are been into by him. The copula blocks it, however transitive the phrase looks.
entries.see also: be up for, be down with, be after

entries.meaning: To leave, to be canceled, to be switched off, to be inaccurate, or to be away from work.
examples: We are off to the airport at six.
They were off before sunrise.
The wedding is off.
The deal was off by the time the lawyers called back.
Make sure the burners are off.
The power was off all night.
Your totals are off by about two hundred dollars.
Something about the story was off from the start.
I am off on Tuesday.
She has been off since the baby came.
In London they'll tell you the milk is off; in Ohio it has gone bad.

senses.head: Leave, set out
body: Announcing your own departure or somebody else's. (уходить, отправляться)
examples: We are off to the airport at six.
They were off before sunrise.

senses.head: Be canceled
body: Of an event or a deal that had been arranged. The opposite is be on. (отменяться, расстроиться)
examples: The wedding is off.
The deal was off by the time the lawyers called back.

senses.head: Be switched off or disconnected
body: Of lights, engines, and utilities. (быть выключенным, отключённым)
examples: Make sure the burners are off.
The power was off all night.

senses.head: Be wrong, be inaccurate
body: Of figures, and of anything that feels not quite right. (быть неточным, не сходиться)
examples: Your totals are off by about two hundred dollars.
Something about the story was off from the start.

senses.head: Be away from work
body: Of a day, a week, or a leave. (быть свободным, не работать)
examples: I am off on Tuesday.
She has been off since the baby came.

senses.head: Be spoiled — British
body: Of food gone bad. An American says the milk has gone bad, not ✗ the milk is off. (испортиться — о продуктах)
examples: In London they'll tell you the milk is off; in Ohio it has gone bad.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: уходить; отменяться; быть выключенным; быть неточным; не работать (о выходном)
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place. ✗ be the wedding off as a statement.
entries.verb type: stative in senses 2 to 6 — canceled (the wedding is off), switched off, inaccurate, on leave, spoiled. Sense 1 (I'm off, he was off before dawn) reports a departure but still takes plain be: ✗ I am being off.
entries.passive: no — no object in any sense, and no passive of be: ✗ the wedding was been off.
entries.see also: be on, be out, be over

entries.meaning: To be going ahead as planned, to be switched on, to be performing or broadcasting, or to be taking a drug.
examples: The game is on despite the rain.
Is the meeting still on for Thursday?
The porch light was on all night.
Leave the fan on.
You are on in five minutes.
The news was on when I walked in.
She is on antibiotics for another week.
He has been on the same blood-pressure pill for years.
Dinner is on me tonight.
Fifty bucks says he misses. — You are on.

senses.head: Be happening, be going ahead
body: The opposite of be off. (идти, состояться)
examples: The game is on despite the rain.
Is the meeting still on for Thursday?

senses.head: Be switched on
body: Of lights, appliances, and engines. (быть включённым)
examples: The porch light was on all night.
Leave the fan on.

senses.head: Be performing or broadcasting
body: Of a performer about to go up, or of a program showing. (выступать; идти — о передаче)
examples: You are on in five minutes.
The news was on when I walked in.

senses.head: Be taking a medication or a drug
body: The substance follows directly. (принимать, сидеть на)
examples: She is on antibiotics for another week.
He has been on the same blood-pressure pill for years.

senses.head: Fixed uses: it's on me, you're on
body: It's on me offers to pay; you're on accepts a bet or a challenge. (я угощаю; идёт, по рукам)
examples: Dinner is on me tonight.
Fifty bucks says he misses. — You are on.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: идти, состояться; быть включённым; выступать; принимать (лекарство)
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place. ✗ be the game on as a statement.
entries.verb type: stative — happening (the game is on), switched on, showing, or taking a drug are all states, as are the fixed it's on me and you're on. ✗ the game is being on.
entries.passive: no — objectless and copular: ✗ the game was been on. Even sense 4, she is on lithium, cannot invert.
entries.see also: be off, be up, be out

entries.meaning: To have figured out what someone is up to, or — with something — to have hit on a promising idea. Often written as one word: onto.
examples: Don't try it twice — they are on to you.
By March the auditors were on to him.
Keep digging — I think you are on to something.
She was on to something big and knew it.
The first draft was noise, but the second was on to something.

senses.head: Have seen through someone
body: Of anybody who has caught on to a scheme. (раскусить, разгадать)
examples: Don't try it twice — they are on to you.
By March the auditors were on to him.

senses.head: Be onto something
body: Have a promising lead or idea. Almost always with the vague word something. (напасть на что-то стоящее)
examples: Keep digging — I think you are on to something.
She was on to something big and knew it.
The first draft was noise, but the second was on to something.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on on, the first of the two particles
entries.русский: раскусить, разгадать; напасть на верный след
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ be him on to, ✗ be it on to.
entries.verb type: stative — a state of knowledge: having seen through someone (the cops are on to him) or having a promising lead (you might be on to something). ✗ they are being on to him.
entries.passive: no — ✗ he is been on to by the cops. Compare the ordinary verb suspect, which does passivize.
entries.see also: be after, be in on, be up to

entries.meaning: To be absent, to have been released, to be unfashionable, to be extinguished, to be ruled out, or to be openly gay.
examples: She is out until Thursday.
The whole crew was out with food poisoning.
The new edition is out in April.
His album has been out for a month.
Cargo shorts are out again, apparently.
The fire was out by midnight.
A June wedding is out — the venue is booked.
He has been out since college.
He was out before the medics reached him.

senses.head: Be absent, be away
body: Of a person away from a desk, a class, or a job. (отсутствовать, выйти)
examples: She is out until Thursday.
The whole crew was out with food poisoning.

senses.head: Be published or released
body: Of books, albums, films, and reports. (выйти, поступить в продажу)
examples: The new edition is out in April.
His album has been out for a month.

senses.head: Be unfashionable
body: The opposite of be in. (выйти из моды)
examples: Cargo shorts are out again, apparently.

senses.head: Be extinguished
body: Of fires, candles, and lights. (погаснуть, потухнуть)
examples: The fire was out by midnight.

senses.head: Be ruled out, be no longer possible
body: Of a plan that has stopped being an option. (отпадать, исключаться)
examples: A June wedding is out — the venue is booked.

senses.head: Be openly gay
body: Of a person who no longer hides it. (не скрывать ориентацию, быть открытым геем)
examples: He has been out since college.

senses.head: Be unconscious
body: Usually intensified: out cold. (быть без сознания)
examples: He was out before the medics reached him.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: отсутствовать; выйти (о книге); выйти из моды; погаснуть; отпасть
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place. ✗ be the book out as a statement.
entries.verb type: stative across all seven senses — absent, published, unfashionable, extinguished, ruled out, openly gay, unconscious. Each is a resulting condition, never an act: ✗ the fire is being out.
entries.passive: no — nothing to promote, and be has no passive: ✗ the book was been out in March.
entries.see also: be in, be off, be out of

entries.meaning: To have no more of something left.
examples: We are out of milk again.
The pharmacy was out of the generic, so I paid for the brand name.
By Friday they were out of clean uniforms.
Tell me before we are out of printer paper, not after.
The store has been out of that model since June.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on out, the first of the two particles
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ be milk out of, ✗ be it out of.
entries.verb type: stative — having none of something left is a state of the subject, not an event: the store has been out of that model since June. ✗ we are being out of milk.
entries.passive: no — ✗ milk is been out of by us. The thing you have run out of can never become the subject.
entries.see also: be out, be in for, be down with

entries.meaning: To be finished; or, of a person, to have gotten past a hurt or an attachment.
examples: The meeting is over.
By the time we parked, the first period was over.
It was over before anyone understood what had happened.
She is over him.
He says he is over it, but he brings it up every week.

senses.head: Be finished, be at an end
body: Of meetings, games, seasons, and relationships seen from outside. (закончиться, кончиться)
examples: The meeting is over.
By the time we parked, the first period was over.
It was over before anyone understood what had happened.

senses.head: No longer be upset about or attached to someone
body: The object is a person or a hurt. (пережить, разлюбить, забыть)
examples: She is over him.
He says he is over it, but he brings it up every week.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional verb in sense 2
entries.separable: no — sense 1 has no object at all, and in sense 2 the person follows the whole phrase: she is over him, never ✗ she is him over.
entries.transitive: either — no object in sense 1, always an object in sense 2
entries.verb type: stative in both senses — an end reached (the meeting is over) and an attachment given up (she is over him). ✗ the meeting is being over, ✗ she is being over him.
entries.passive: no — sense 1 has no object, and sense 2's object resists promotion: ✗ he is been over by her.
entries.see also: be through, be off, break up

entries.meaning: To have finished a task, or to have ended a relationship or a job for good.
examples: Call me when you are through.
We were through with the inventory by noon.
She is through with him.
After that meeting he was through at the firm.
I am through apologizing for it.

senses.head: Have finished a task
body: Of work that is done. (закончить, справиться)
examples: Call me when you are through.
We were through with the inventory by noon.

senses.head: Have ended a relationship or an association
body: Final in tone: it means there will be no going back. (порвать, покончить)
examples: She is through with him.
After that meeting he was through at the firm.
I am through apologizing for it.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); with an object it takes with
entries.separable: no — what you are finished with follows with: I am through with the report, never ✗ I am through the report with.
entries.transitive: either — no object alone, or an object after with
entries.verb type: stative — a state of completion (I'm through with the report) or of a relationship finally ended (we're through). ✗ I am being through with it.
entries.passive: no — ✗ the report is been through with. What you are finished with stays inside the with-phrase.
entries.see also: be over, be off, break up

entries.meaning: To be awake and out of bed, to have expired, to be going on, to be higher than before, or to be running.
examples: She is up at five every morning.
Were you up when the storm hit?
Time is up.
The lease was up in March.
What is up with the elevator?
Something was up — the whole floor had gone quiet.
Rents are up eleven percent.
We were up by two with a minute left.
The site is up again.

senses.head: Be awake and out of bed
body: Not merely conscious — up and moving. (встать, не спать)
examples: She is up at five every morning.
Were you up when the storm hit?

senses.head: Have expired
body: Of time, a lease, or a term. (истечь, кончиться — о сроке)
examples: Time is up.
The lease was up in March.

senses.head: Be happening, be the matter
body: Usually the question what's up. (происходить, случиться)
examples: What is up with the elevator?
Something was up — the whole floor had gone quiet.

senses.head: Be higher, be ahead
body: Of prices and of a score. (вырасти, подняться; вести в счёте)
examples: Rents are up eleven percent.
We were up by two with a minute left.

senses.head: Be running, be online
body: Of a site, a server, or a system that is working again. (работать, быть доступным)
examples: The site is up again.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: не спать, встать; истечь (о времени); происходить; вырасти
entries.separable: not applicable — there is no object to place. ✗ be the site up as a statement.
entries.verb type: stative — awake (she's up), expired (time is up), afoot (what's up), higher (sales are up), running (the site is up again). All conditions: ✗ the site is being up.
entries.passive: no — intransitive and copular: ✗ the lease was been up in March.
entries.see also: be down, be up for, be up to

entries.meaning: To be willing and eager to do something, or to be a candidate for something.
examples: Are you up for a hike Saturday?
Nobody was up for another meeting.
The contract is up for renewal in June.
Two of the judges are up for re-election.
Her name was up for the fellowship twice.
He is up for his third DUI.

senses.head: Be willing, be in the mood for
body: Informal, and usually a question or an invitation. (быть готовым, быть не против)
examples: Are you up for a hike Saturday?
Nobody was up for another meeting.

senses.head: Be a candidate for, be due for
body: Of contracts, elections, awards, and reviews. (выдвигаться, подлежать)
examples: The contract is up for renewal in June.
Two of the judges are up for re-election.
Her name was up for the fellowship twice.

senses.head: Be on trial for
body: Informal, in police and courthouse talk. (быть под судом за)
examples: He is up for his third DUI.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on up; for is reduced to a schwa
entries.русский: быть готовым, быть не против; выдвигаться, подлежать (рассмотрению)
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ be a hike up for, ✗ be it up for.
entries.verb type: stative — willingness (are you up for a hike), candidacy (the contract is up for renewal), or standing trial (he's up for burglary). ✗ I am being up for it.
entries.passive: no — ✗ a hike is been up for by me. The renewal sense already reads passively in meaning, but the form cannot change.
entries.see also: be up, be up to, be in for

entries.meaning: To be doing something (usually something you shouldn't), to be capable of something, or to be somebody's decision.
examples: What are those two up to?
He was up to something all week and wouldn't say what.
She isn't up to a long drive yet.
Are you up to company tonight?
Where we eat is up to you.
It was up to the board, and the board said no.

senses.head: Be doing something, usually sneaky
body: The suspicion is built into the phrase; what are you up to is rarely a neutral question. (замышлять, затевать)
examples: What are those two up to?
He was up to something all week and wouldn't say what.

senses.head: Be capable of, feel well enough for
body: Usually negative or in a question. (быть в состоянии, быть по силам)
examples: She isn't up to a long drive yet.
Are you up to company tonight?

senses.head: Be somebody's decision or responsibility
body: The person deciding follows to. (зависеть от, решать)
examples: Where we eat is up to you.
It was up to the board, and the board said no.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on up, the first of the two particles
entries.русский: замышлять, затевать; быть в состоянии; зависеть от, решать
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ be something up to, ✗ be it up to.
entries.verb type: stative — even sense 1, which describes activity, uses plain be: what are you up to?, never ✗ what are you being up to? Senses 2 and 3 (capability, responsibility) are plainly states.
entries.passive: no — ✗ something is been up to by him; ✗ the decision is been up to her.
entries.see also: be up, be up for, be on to

entries.meaning: To press harder physically, to push during childbirth, or to redouble your effort.
examples: You have to bear down or the carbon copy won't take.
He bore down until the bolt finally turned.
The nurse told her to bear down and count to ten.
The team bore down in the fourth quarter.
If we bear down now, we can ship on Friday.

senses.head: Press harder
body: Of a hand, a pen, or a tool. (нажать сильнее, надавить)
examples: You have to bear down or the carbon copy won't take.
He bore down until the bolt finally turned.

senses.head: Push during labor
body: The standard delivery-room instruction, and a fixed use. (тужиться)
examples: The nurse told her to bear down and count to ten.

senses.head: Redouble your effort
body: Of a team or a worker in the last stretch. (поднажать, собраться)
examples: The team bore down in the fourth quarter.
If we bear down now, we can ship on Friday.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — bear down takes no object; whatever is under the pressure goes after on (see bear down on). ✗ bear the pedal down.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: pressing harder on a pen, pushing in labor, redoubling effort. The progressive is normal: she was bearing down on the last mile.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; whatever takes the pressure appears only after on (see bear down on): ✗ the pedal was borne down.
entries.see also: bear down on, bear up, bear out

entries.meaning: To move toward something in a way that looks threatening, or to put heavy pressure on someone.
examples: The truck was bearing down on us before he touched the horn.
A second storm is bearing down on the coast.
He bore down on the wrench with both hands.
Corporate has been bearing down on the branch managers all quarter.
The bank bore down on him for two missed payments.

senses.head: Move menacingly toward
body: Of storms, trucks, and anything large closing the distance. (надвигаться на, нестись на)
examples: The truck was bearing down on us before he touched the horn.
A second storm is bearing down on the coast.

senses.head: Press hard on physically
body: Of a hand or a tool against a surface. (давить на, налегать на)
examples: He bore down on the wrench with both hands.

senses.head: Put pressure on someone
body: Of management, regulators, or creditors. (наседать на, давить на)
examples: Corporate has been bearing down on the branch managers all quarter.
The bank bore down on him for two missed payments.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on down, the first of the two particles
entries.русский: надвигаться на, нестись на; давить на, наседать
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ bear the storm down on us, ✗ bear it down on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: a storm closing the distance, a hand pressing on a surface, regulators applying pressure. Progressive is the usual form: the truck was bearing down on us.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive works in the pressure sense (the department has been borne down on by regulators all year) but sounds forced with weather or traffic: ✗ we were borne down on by the storm.
entries.see also: bear down, bear on, beat down

entries.meaning: To be relevant to something. Bear upon is the same verb one degree more formal, and both belong to writing rather than speech.
examples: None of that bears on the question before the court.
The new findings bear directly on how we read the earlier data.
Two facts bear on the decision, and only two.
Explain how the memo bears upon the timeline.
Whatever bore on her choice, she never explained it.
entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ bear the question on. An adverb may slip in (bears directly on the case), but an object never can.
entries.verb type: stative — it states a relation of relevance, not an event: two facts bear on the decision. The progressive is out: ✗ these findings are bearing on the case.
entries.passive: no — stative relations resist the prepositional passive: ✗ the question is borne on by none of that, ✗ the timeline was borne upon by the memo.
entries.see also: bear down on, bear out, bear with

entries.meaning: To confirm that something claimed or predicted is in fact true.
examples: The data bear out what the field crews had been saying for months.
Every audit since then has borne out her account.
If the tests bear the theory out, the paper gets published.
I checked the receipts, and they bear him out.
His story didn't hold up — nothing in the log bore it out.
Later events bore out a warning nobody had wanted to hear.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — the numbers bear out his claim or the numbers bear his claim out, and with a pronoun the object must split: the numbers bear it out, never ✗ bear out it.
entries.verb type: action with a stative flavor — it names the confirming, so the perfect is common (every audit has borne out her account) but the progressive is odd: ✗ the data are bearing out his claim.
entries.passive: yes, and it is frequent — her account was borne out by every audit since, his story wasn't borne out by anything in the log. Note the participle borne, not ✗ born.
entries.see also: bear on, bear up, bring out

entries.meaning: To keep going without collapsing under strain.
examples: She is bearing up better than anyone expected.
He bore up through two years of treatment.
How are you bearing up?
The family has borne up remarkably well.
The old bridge bore up under traffic it was never designed for.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — bear up takes no object; what you are enduring follows under. ✗ bear the strain up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative, describing someone holding out under strain, so the progressive is idiomatic: she is bearing up better than anyone expected.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; the strain follows under and cannot be promoted: ✗ the traffic was borne up under by the bridge.
entries.see also: bear with, bear down, bear out

entries.meaning: To be patient with someone or something. Most often heard as the request bear with me.
examples: Bear with me — the file is still loading.
Please bear with us while the system updates.
She bore with his complaints for three years.
If you can bear with the noise, the apartment is a bargain.
Thanks for bearing with us during the remodel.
entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ bear me with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, describing patience extended over a stretch of time: thanks for bearing with us during the remodel. Most often an imperative appeal, bear with me.
entries.passive: no — the object of with stays put: ✗ we were borne with by the customers, ✗ his complaints were borne with by her (the plain transitive bore works instead).
entries.see also: bear up, bear on, be through

entries.meaning: To force an attack, a fire, or a challenge to retreat.
examples: Crews beat back the fire before it reached the ridge.
The defenders beat the assault back twice in one night.
They beat them back as far as the tree line.
She has beaten back every challenge to the ruling.
The company beat back a hostile takeover in 2019.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — beat back the flames or beat the flames back, and a pronoun must split: beat them back, never ✗ beat back them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and resultative: an attack or a fire is driven back to somewhere it was not. Progressive is fine: crews were beating back the flames all night.
entries.passive: yes — the flames were beaten back by dawn, the amendment was beaten back in committee.
entries.see also: beat off, beat down, beat out

entries.meaning: Of the sun or rain, to come down hard; of a person, to force something down — a door, a price, or somebody's spirit.
examples: The sun beat down on the parking lot all afternoon.
Rain was beating down by the time we reached the car.
They beat down the door with a battering ram.
The wind beat the back fence down.
He beat the dealer down four hundred dollars.
She beat it down to nine hundred and walked out happy.
Two years of that shift beat him down.

senses.head: Come down hard
body: Of sun or rain, and always without an object. (палить, хлестать)
examples: The sun beat down on the parking lot all afternoon.
Rain was beating down by the time we reached the car.

senses.head: Force open
body: Of a door or a fence. (выломать, выбить)
examples: They beat down the door with a battering ram.
The wind beat the back fence down.

senses.head: Bargain someone lower
body: Informal, of a price or a seller. (сбить цену)
examples: He beat the dealer down four hundred dollars.
She beat it down to nine hundred and walked out happy.

senses.head: Break someone's spirit
body: Of a job, an illness, or a long defeat. (сломить, задавить)
examples: Two years of that shift beat him down.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: палить (о солнце); выломать; сбить цену; сломить
entries.separable: yes in the transitive senses — beat down the price or beat the price down, and a pronoun must split: beat it down. Sense 1, about the sun, has no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — no object in sense 1, an object in the rest
entries.verb type: action in every sense — the sun coming down hard (sense 1), forcing a door, bargaining a price lower, breaking someone's spirit. Progressive throughout: the sun was beating down.
entries.passive: yes in senses 2 to 4 — the door had been beaten down, the price was beaten down to nine hundred, he was beaten down by two years of it. No passive of sense 1: ✗ we were beaten down on by the sun.
entries.see also: beat back, beat up, bear down on

entries.meaning: To drive off an attacker or a rival; in American slang the same two words also mean to masturbate.
examples: They beat off two counterattacks that morning.
The incumbent beat off three challengers in the primary.
She beat them off with a boat oar.
Half the class snickered, because beat off is also vulgar slang.
A copy editor will change beat off to fight off for exactly that reason.

senses.head: Drive off an attack or a rival
body: Of armies, animals, and competitors. (отбить, отразить)
examples: They beat off two counterattacks that morning.
The incumbent beat off three challengers in the primary.
She beat them off with a boat oar.

senses.head: Masturbate — vulgar slang
body: Male slang, common enough in American speech that the standard sense can raise a snicker. (вульг.: дрочить)
examples: Half the class snickered, because beat off is also vulgar slang.
A copy editor will change beat off to fight off for exactly that reason.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes in sense 1 — beat off the attack or beat the attack off, and a pronoun must split: beat it off. Sense 2 takes no object.
entries.transitive: either — an object in sense 1, none in sense 2
entries.register: everyday — sense 1 is standard; sense 2 is vulgar slang, which is why careful writers often choose fight off instead
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both: driving back an attack or a rival (sense 1) and the vulgar slang sense 2, which describes an act, not a state.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1 — the assault was beaten off with heavy losses, the takeover bid was beaten off. No in sense 2, which takes no object: ✗ it was beaten off by him.
entries.see also: beat back, beat out, beat up

entries.meaning: To defeat somebody narrowly, to put out a fire by hitting it, or to tap out a rhythm.
examples: She beat out nine other applicants.
They beat us out by a tenth of a second.
He beat them out for the last roster spot.
He beat out the flames with his jacket.
Somebody was beating out a rhythm on the bar.
He beat out the throw to first.

senses.head: Defeat narrowly, edge out
body: Of applicants, rivals, and racers. (обойти, опередить)
examples: She beat out nine other applicants.
They beat us out by a tenth of a second.
He beat them out for the last roster spot.

senses.head: Put out a fire by hitting it
body: Of flames smothered with a coat or a blanket. (сбить, затушить)
examples: He beat out the flames with his jacket.

senses.head: Tap out a rhythm
body: Of drumming on any surface. (выстукивать, отбивать)
examples: Somebody was beating out a rhythm on the bar.

senses.head: Baseball: reach base ahead of the throw
body: A fixed use in American sports talk. (успеть добежать)
examples: He beat out the throw to first.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — beat out the competition or beat the competition out, and a pronoun must split: beat them out, never ✗ beat out them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic in all four senses: edging out a rival, smothering a fire, tapping a rhythm, reaching base ahead of the throw.
entries.passive: yes — she was beaten out by a candidate with more experience, the fire was beaten out with a coat, the rhythm was beaten out on the tailgate.
entries.see also: beat back, beat up on, beat off

entries.meaning: To hit someone repeatedly and hurt them; with a reflexive pronoun, to blame yourself.
examples: Three of them beat up a kid over a bike.
They beat him up and took his phone.
He got beaten up outside the bar.
Don't beat yourself up over one bad quarter.
She has been beating herself up about it since Friday.
He drives a beat-up Corolla with one gray door.

senses.head: Assault physically
body: Of a beating, usually by more than one person. (избить, поколотить)
examples: Three of them beat up a kid over a bike.
They beat him up and took his phone.
He got beaten up outside the bar.

senses.head: Blame yourself
body: Always reflexive: beat yourself up, and the pronoun sits in the middle. (корить себя, есть себя поедом)
examples: Don't beat yourself up over one bad quarter.
She has been beating herself up about it since Friday.

senses.head: Beat-up as an adjective
body: Hyphenated before a noun, it means battered and worn. (побитый, потрёпанный)
examples: He drives a beat-up Corolla with one gray door.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — beat up the guy or beat the guy up, and a pronoun must split: beat him up, never ✗ beat up him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 2 (assault; the reflexive beat yourself up). Sense 3 is no longer a verb at all but the attributive adjective beat-up: a beat-up Corolla.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1 — he was beaten up outside the bar. No passive of the reflexive sense 2: ✗ himself was beaten up by him — say he beat himself up over it.
entries.see also: beat up on, beat down, bust up

entries.meaning: To attack someone repeatedly, physically or in words; in sports, to beat a weak opponent badly.
examples: The columnists have been beating up on the mayor all week.
Quit beating up on your brother.
They beat up on the worst team in the league and called it a statement.
It's easy to beat up on the people who aren't in the room.
He beat up on himself for weeks after the trade.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on up, the first of the two particles
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. ✗ beat the mayor up on, ✗ beat him up on.
entries.register: informal — American; British English has no up on here
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and typically iterative, which is why the progressive is so common: the columnists have been beating up on the mayor all week.
entries.passive: restricted — natural enough in the criticism sense (the mayor has been beaten up on all week), stiff with an agent: ✗ your brother was beaten up on by you.
entries.see also: beat up, beat down, bear down on

entries.meaning: To happen to someone or something — used only in questions about a fate nobody has followed up on.
examples: Whatever became of the couple who lived upstairs?
What has become of the original blueprints?
What will become of the shop once she retires?
Nobody knows what became of the second set of keys.
What is to become of these kids if the program closes?
entries.pronunciation note: unusually for a phrasal verb, the stress can sit on either word; the phrase is frozen either way
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ become the shop of.
entries.register: everyday — but frozen: it appears only in questions with what or whatever
entries.verb type: stative — it reports a fate, and only inside a what/whatever question: whatever became of the couple upstairs? No progressive: ✗ what is becoming of the blueprints?
entries.passive: no — become has no passive in any of its uses, this one included: ✗ the shop was become of, ✗ the keys were become of by nobody.
entries.see also: be around, be over

entries.meaning: To take something as the first item; and in the fixed phrase to begin with, to mean 'in the first place'.
examples: Let's begin with the numbers and work backward.
The book begins with a funeral and never gets lighter.
Every class begins with ten minutes of review.
To begin with, nobody asked whether she wanted the job.
There were only four of us to begin with.

senses.head: Start with something
body: Of an order of business, a book, or a routine. (начинать с, начинаться с)
examples: Let's begin with the numbers and work backward.
The book begins with a funeral and never gets lighter.
Every class begins with ten minutes of review.

senses.head: To begin with — in the first place
body: A frozen adverbial that either opens an objection or points back to how things started. (для начала; изначально)
examples: To begin with, nobody asked whether she wanted the job.
There were only four of us to begin with.

entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.русский: начинать с, начинаться с; для начала
entries.separable: no — what you start with follows with: begin with the basics, never ✗ begin the basics with. When begin has an object of its own, with still comes after it: begin the class with a review.
entries.verb type: action in sense 1 — dynamic and inceptive: begin with the basics, the book begins with a funeral. Sense 2, to begin with, is a frozen adverbial, not a verb phrase you can inflect.
entries.passive: restricted — the passive belongs to begin plus its own object, not to begin with: the meeting was begun with a moment of silence (formal) is fine, but ✗ the basics were begun with.
entries.see also: break into, burst into, bring up

entries.meaning: To make an enormous effort to help or accommodate someone.
examples: They bent over backward to get us on an earlier flight.
She has bent over backwards for that family for ten years.
I bent over backward to keep the meeting civil.
The school will bend over backward to avoid a lawsuit.
He bends over backward for strangers and forgets his own family.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on backward, the last word of the frozen phrase
entries.русский: из кожи вон лезть, лезть из кожи
entries.separable: no — the phrase is frozen, and whoever you are helping goes after for or into a to-clause. ✗ bend me over backward, ✗ bend over me backward.
entries.transitive: no — it takes for plus a person, or to plus a verb
entries.register: everyday — Americans say both backward and backwards
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and idiomatic, describing effort made: they bent over backward to accommodate us. The progressive is normal: he is bending over backward for these people.
entries.passive: no — the idiom takes no object at all; the person helped sits behind for: ✗ we were bent over backward for by them.
entries.see also: bear with, bear up, bring around

entries.meaning: To wager that something will fail, or to expect someone to lose.
examples: Two funds made a fortune betting against the housing market.
Never bet against a team with nothing to lose.
I wouldn't bet against her.
They bet against their own clients and got sued for it.
Analysts who bet against the merger were right for once.
entries.pronunciation note: either word can carry the stress; against, being two syllables, takes it easily
entries.русский: ставить против; не верить в успех
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ bet the market against.
entries.register: everyday — very common in writing about money and sports
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, whether the money is real (bet against the Yankees) or the sense is figurative (never bet against her).
entries.passive: restricted — financial writing allows it (the housing market was heavily bet against in 2007), but ordinary speech does not: ✗ she was bet against by nobody — say nobody bet against her.
entries.see also: bet on, buy into

entries.meaning: To wager money on an outcome, or — more often in speech — to count on something happening.
examples: He bet two hundred on the Rams.
Nobody was betting on the underdog that week.
Will the flight be on time? Don't bet on it.
I wouldn't bet on him showing up before ten.
She'll be there. You can bet on it.

senses.head: Wager money on
body: The literal sense, with the stake before on. (ставить на)
examples: He bet two hundred on the Rams.
Nobody was betting on the underdog that week.

senses.head: Count on, be confident about
body: Usually negative: don't bet on it, I wouldn't bet on it. (рассчитывать на, полагаться)
examples: Will the flight be on time? Don't bet on it.
I wouldn't bet on him showing up before ten.

senses.head: You can bet on it — a promise
body: A set phrase amounting to 'you have my word'. (можешь быть уверен)
examples: She'll be there. You can bet on it.

entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.separable: no — what you are betting on always follows on. An amount may come first (bet fifty on the gray horse), but the thing itself never moves: ✗ bet the gray horse on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in sense 1 (wagering) and sense 2 (counting on something). Sense 3, you can bet on it, is a frozen promise and does not inflect freely.
entries.passive: restricted — the literal wager passivizes stiffly: the gray horse was heavily bet on is possible in racing talk. The confidence sense does not: ✗ it was not bet on by me — say I wouldn't bet on it.
entries.see also: bet against, buy into

entries.meaning: In criminal procedure, to order that a defendant be held for trial in a higher court.
examples: The judge bound the defendant over for trial.
He was bound over on two felony counts.
The magistrate bound them over after a two-hour hearing.
The case was bound over to the grand jury in March.
Prosecutors asked the court to bind over all four suspects.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: передать дело в суд, обязать явиться в суд
entries.separable: yes — bind over the defendant or bind the defendant over, and a pronoun must split: bound him over, never ✗ bound over him.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object, and usually in the passive
entries.register: formal — American courtroom vocabulary; outside a legal report people say send to trial
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, a court act with a result: the defendant is now held for trial. Legal register, and the perfect and past dominate: the magistrate bound them over.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the ordinary form — he was bound over on two felony counts, the case was bound over to the grand jury in March.
entries.see also: bind up, bring in

entries.meaning: To bandage or tie something tightly; in the passive, to be inseparably connected with something or absorbed in it.
examples: She bound up his arm with a strip of shirt.
He bound the wound up as best he could.
Bind it up until the medics get here.
The town's fortunes are bound up with the mill.
Her whole identity was bound up with the job.
He is so bound up in the case that he forgets to eat.

senses.head: Bandage, tie tightly
body: Literary, and mostly met in older writing. (перевязать, забинтовать)
examples: She bound up his arm with a strip of shirt.
He bound the wound up as best he could.
Bind it up until the medics get here.

senses.head: Be bound up with — be inseparably connected
body: Frozen in the passive. (быть тесно связанным с)
examples: The town's fortunes are bound up with the mill.
Her whole identity was bound up with the job.

senses.head: Be bound up in — be absorbed in
body: Also frozen, and about attention rather than connection. (быть поглощённым чем-то)
examples: He is so bound up in the case that he forgets to eat.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: перевязать, забинтовать; быть тесно связанным с
entries.separable: yes in sense 1 — bind up the wound or bind the wound up, and a pronoun must split: bind it up. The passive be bound up with in senses 2 and 3 is frozen and never splits.
entries.register: formal — sense 1 is literary; an American doctor says bandage
entries.verb type: action in sense 1 — dynamic and literary: bind up the wound. Senses 2 and 3 survive only as frozen passive participles behaving like adjectives: bound up with, bound up in.
entries.passive: yes — the wound was bound up before the doctor arrived. Senses 2 and 3 exist in the passive alone: her fate is bound up with his, he was bound up in the campaign, with no active ✗ the war bound up her fate with his.
entries.see also: bind over, build up

entries.meaning: To hold in something you were about to say, or to hit back at whoever attacked you.
examples: She bit back the obvious reply.
He bit it back and said nothing.
I bit back a laugh and nodded.
The union bit back with an ad campaign of its own.
Inflation bit back two quarters later.

senses.head: Suppress a remark or a reaction
body: Of the obvious reply you decide not to make. (сдержать, проглотить — слова)
examples: She bit back the obvious reply.
He bit it back and said nothing.
I bit back a laugh and nodded.

senses.head: Retaliate
body: Of a person, an institution, or an economic force hitting back. (огрызнуться, дать сдачи)
examples: The union bit back with an ad campaign of its own.
Inflation bit back two quarters later.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes in sense 1 — bite back a retort or bite a retort back, and a pronoun must split: bite it back. Sense 2 takes no object.
entries.transitive: either — an object in sense 1, none in sense 2
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both: suppressing a remark (sense 1) and retaliating (sense 2). Progressive is fine either way: she was biting back a laugh.
entries.passive: restricted — sense 1 passivizes awkwardly: the retort was bitten back is grammatical but stilted. Sense 2 has no object and so no passive at all: ✗ the market was bitten back by.
entries.see also: bite off, bite into, beat back

entries.meaning: To sink your teeth into something, or — of costs and losses — to eat away at it.
examples: He bit into the sandwich and stopped talking.
Bite into one and tell me it isn't out of a can.
Fuel costs are biting into margins.
The renovation bit into our savings faster than we planned.
The strap bit into his shoulder.

senses.head: Sink your teeth into
body: The literal sense. (вгрызться, откусить)
examples: He bit into the sandwich and stopped talking.
Bite into one and tell me it isn't out of a can.

senses.head: Eat away at money, time, or profit
body: Of costs, taxes, and delays. (съедать, урезать)
examples: Fuel costs are biting into margins.
The renovation bit into our savings faster than we planned.

senses.head: Cut into a surface
body: Of a rope, a strap, or a blade. (врезаться)
examples: The strap bit into his shoulder.

entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.русский: вгрызться в, откусить; съедать, урезать; врезаться
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ bite the apple into.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three: sinking teeth in, costs eating away at profit, a strap cutting a shoulder. Progressive is normal: the rope was biting into his hands.
entries.passive: restricted — the literal sense allows a prepositional passive in the perfect (every cupcake had been bitten into), and the money sense is heavy but attested: profits were badly bitten into by fuel costs. Avoid it with the cutting sense: ✗ his shoulder was bitten into by the strap.
entries.see also: bite off, bite back, burn through

entries.meaning: To remove a piece with your teeth; and in the fixed idiom, to take on more than you can handle.
examples: He bit off the end of the cigar.
She bit the tag off rather than look for scissors.
Bite it off — don't pull.
With three renovations at once, they bit off more than they could chew.
Don't bite off more than you can chew in your first semester.

senses.head: Remove with the teeth
body: The literal sense. (откусить)
examples: He bit off the end of the cigar.
She bit the tag off rather than look for scissors.
Bite it off — don't pull.

senses.head: Bite off more than you can chew
body: A fixed idiom about overcommitting. (взвалить на себя слишком много)
examples: With three renovations at once, they bit off more than they could chew.
Don't bite off more than you can chew in your first semester.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: откусить; взвалить на себя слишком много
entries.separable: yes — bite off a piece or bite a piece off, and a pronoun must split: bite it off, never ✗ bite off it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic: he bit off the cap and spat it out. Sense 2 is the fixed idiom bite off more than you can chew, which resists any reshaping.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1 — the cap had been bitten off, two of the buttons were bitten off. The idiom keeps its active shape: ✗ more than he could chew was bitten off by him.
entries.see also: bite into, bite back, build up

entries.meaning: To take every last dollar or resource out of somebody.
examples: The legal fees bled the company dry.
Two divorces bled him dry.
They will bleed you dry if you let them bill by the hour.
The war bled the treasury dry.
He has been bled dry by his own relatives.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on dry, the word that completes the idiom
entries.separable: the object has no choice — it sits between the two words: bleed the company dry, bleed them dry. ✗ bleed dry the company.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and resultative: dry is a result predicate on the object, so the pattern is verb + object + complement (bleed the company dry), close to but not the same as a linking use.
entries.passive: yes — he has been bled dry by his own relatives, the treasury was bled dry by four years of war. The complement dry travels with the verb.
entries.see also: bleed out, bleed off, burn through

entries.meaning: To release a fluid, a gas, or a resource slowly and on purpose.
examples: Bleed off the pressure before you open the valve.
The crew bled the excess off through a second line.
Bleed it off in stages, not all at once.
The fund quietly bled off cash for two years.
A leaky seal had been bleeding off coolant since spring.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — bleed off the pressure or bleed the pressure off, and a pronoun must split: bleed it off.
entries.register: everyday — technical: plumbing, aviation, and finance; in ordinary speech Americans say let out or drain
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, deliberate, and gradual, which suits the progressive: a leaky seal had been bleeding off coolant since spring.
entries.passive: yes — the pressure was bled off through a second line, cash was quietly bled off for two years.
entries.see also: bleed out, bleed dry, burn off

entries.meaning: To die from blood loss, or to drain a fluid out of a system.
examples: He bled out before the helicopter landed.
Without a tourniquet she would have bled out in minutes.
Bleed out the lines before you cap them.
We bled the radiators out in October.
Bleed it out slowly or you'll get an airlock.

senses.head: Die of blood loss
body: Intransitive, and grim. (истечь кровью)
examples: He bled out before the helicopter landed.
Without a tourniquet she would have bled out in minutes.

senses.head: Drain fluid or air out
body: Of brake lines, radiators, and hydraulic systems. (стравить, спустить)
examples: Bleed out the lines before you cap them.
We bled the radiators out in October.
Bleed it out slowly or you'll get an airlock.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes in sense 2 — bleed out the lines or bleed the lines out, and a pronoun must split: bleed them out. Sense 1 takes no object.
entries.transitive: either — no object in sense 1, an object in sense 2
entries.register: everyday — medical and trade usage; most Americans know sense 1 from hospital shows
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both: dying of blood loss (sense 1) and draining a line (sense 2). Progressive fits either: he was bleeding out on the shoulder of the road.
entries.passive: yes in sense 2 — the brake lines were bled out before the test drive. No in sense 1, which has no object: ✗ he was bled out on the highway means something else entirely.
entries.see also: bleed off, bleed dry, burn out

entries.meaning: To be carried off by wind; to astonish somebody; to defeat somebody easily; and in slang, to shoot dead.
examples: The tarp blew away overnight.
Wind blew the ballots away before anyone could stop it.
Her audition blew us away.
That last chapter blew me away.
They blew away a team that hadn't lost all season.
In the movie he blows away three guys before the credits.

senses.head: Be carried off by wind
body: With or without an object, depending on whether the wind is the subject. (сдуть, унести)
examples: The tarp blew away overnight.
Wind blew the ballots away before anyone could stop it.

senses.head: Astonish, overwhelm
body: Informal, and always with the person as the object in the middle. (потрясти, поразить)
examples: Her audition blew us away.
That last chapter blew me away.

senses.head: Defeat easily
body: Informal, of games and competitions. (разгромить)
examples: They blew away a team that hadn't lost all season.

senses.head: Shoot dead — slang
body: Crime-movie vocabulary. (пристрелить, уложить)
examples: In the movie he blows away three guys before the credits.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: сдуть, унести; потрясти, поразить; разгромить; пристрелить
entries.separable: yes — blow away the competition or blow the competition away, and a pronoun must split: it blew me away, never ✗ it blew away me.
entries.transitive: either — an object in senses 2 to 4, and none when the wind does the work
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four: wind carrying something off, astonishing someone, winning easily, shooting someone dead. Progressive is fine: the tarp was blowing away.
entries.passive: yes — and in sense 2 the passive is the usual form: I was blown away by the ending. Also the roof was blown away, they were blown away in the third quarter, he was blown away in the parking lot.
entries.see also: blow up, blow out, blow over

entries.meaning: To arrive suddenly and without warning — of a person, or of weather.
examples: He blew in around midnight with no explanation.
Look who just blew in.
Cold air blew in off the lake and dropped it ten degrees.
Her cousin blows in every couple of years and stays a week.
The storm blew in faster than the forecast said it would.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — blow in takes no object. ✗ blow him in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, describing an arrival, usually a sudden or unannounced one: he blew in around midnight with no luggage.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ he was blown in at midnight would mean the wind carried him.
entries.see also: blow through, blow over, burst in

entries.meaning: To skip something you were supposed to do, to ignore a person, or to let off pressure.
examples: He blew off two classes and a lab.
She blew the appointment off and rescheduled twice.
I texted him twice and he blew me off.
Don't blow her off — she signs the checks.
He plays pickup hockey to blow off steam.
The blast blew off part of the roof.

senses.head: Skip an obligation
body: Of classes, appointments, and chores. (забить на, прогулять)
examples: He blew off two classes and a lab.
She blew the appointment off and rescheduled twice.

senses.head: Ignore or brush aside a person
body: The person goes in the middle when it is a pronoun. (продинамить, отшить)
examples: I texted him twice and he blew me off.
Don't blow her off — she signs the checks.

senses.head: Blow off steam
body: A fixed phrase for releasing tension. (выпустить пар)
examples: He plays pickup hockey to blow off steam.

senses.head: Detach with force
body: Of wind or an explosion tearing something away. (сорвать, снести)
examples: The blast blew off part of the roof.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: забить на, прогулять; продинамить; выпустить пар
entries.separable: yes — blow off the meeting or blow the meeting off, and a pronoun must split: blow it off, he blew me off, never ✗ blow off it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: skipping an obligation, brushing off a person, releasing tension (blow off steam), and tearing something loose.
entries.passive: yes — the meeting was blown off twice, I was blown off again, the roof was blown off in the storm. The idiom resists it: ✗ steam was blown off by him.
entries.see also: blow up, blow through, blow away

entries.meaning: To put a flame out by blowing; of a tire or a joint, to burst or give way; in sports, to win by a huge margin.
examples: Blow out the candles before you leave.
She blew them out one at a time.
A tire blew out on the interstate.
He blew out his knee in the second quarter.
They blew out the Cardinals 45 to 7.

senses.head: Put out a flame
body: Of candles, matches, and pilot lights. (задуть, потушить)
examples: Blow out the candles before you leave.
She blew them out one at a time.

senses.head: Burst — of a tire
body: Intransitive, and the source of the noun blowout. (лопнуть)
examples: A tire blew out on the interstate.

senses.head: Injure a knee or a shoulder badly
body: American sports usage. (порвать, повредить)
examples: He blew out his knee in the second quarter.

senses.head: Defeat by a wide margin
body: Informal, and usually with a score attached. (разгромить)
examples: They blew out the Cardinals 45 to 7.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: задуть, потушить; лопнуть (о шине); порвать (связку); разгромить
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — blow out the candles or blow the candles out, and a pronoun must split: blow them out. Senses 2 and 3 are used without an object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: extinguishing a flame, a tire bursting (sense 2, intransitive), wrecking a knee, winning by a wide margin.
entries.passive: yes where there is an object — the candles were blown out, his knee was blown out in the second half, they were blown out 42 to 3. No for sense 2: ✗ the tire was blown out by itself — say the tire blew out.
entries.see also: blow up, blow away, blow over

entries.meaning: Of a storm or a scandal, to pass and be forgotten; of wind, to knock something down.
examples: The storm blew over by morning.
Give it a week and the front will blow over.
He kept his head down until it blew over.
These things usually blow over by the next news cycle.
The wind blew the patio umbrella over.
It blew them over like dominoes.

senses.head: Pass, die down
body: Of weather. (пройти, утихнуть)
examples: The storm blew over by morning.
Give it a week and the front will blow over.

senses.head: Be forgotten — of trouble
body: Of scandals and arguments that fade if nobody feeds them. (замяться, забыться)
examples: He kept his head down until it blew over.
These things usually blow over by the next news cycle.

senses.head: Knock down by wind
body: Of anything the wind topples. (повалить, опрокинуть)
examples: The wind blew the patio umbrella over.
It blew them over like dominoes.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes in the knock-down sense — the wind blew over the fence or blew the fence over, and a pronoun must split: blew it over. In the passing-storm sense there is no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: the weather and scandal senses are intransitive happenings (the storm blew over), sense 3 is the causative counterpart (the wind blew the fence over). No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in the knock-down sense, where it is the commonest form — the patio umbrella was blown over in the night, they were blown over like dominoes. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ the storm was blown over, ✗ it was blown over by the next news cycle.
entries.see also: blow in, blow up, blow away

entries.meaning: To use something up fast, or to move through a place or a task quickly.
examples: He blew through the advance in four months.
We blew through two reams of paper on one job.
The front blew through around three.
They blew through the stop sign without slowing.
She blew through the first ten questions.

senses.head: Spend or consume rapidly
body: Of money, supplies, and time. (промотать, просадить)
examples: He blew through the advance in four months.
We blew through two reams of paper on one job.

senses.head: Move through quickly
body: Of weather fronts, drivers, and travelers. (пронестись, промчаться)
examples: The front blew through around three.
They blew through the stop sign without slowing.

senses.head: Get through work fast
body: Of an easy task. (пролететь, быстро справиться)
examples: She blew through the first ten questions.

entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.русский: промотать, просадить; пронестись через; пролететь (по заданию)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ blow the money through, ✗ blow it through.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses, of spending, of moving fast, and of racing through work. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — a prepositional passive is possible in the spending sense (the advance was blown through in four months) but sounds odd, and the active is standard. The movement senses have none: ✗ the stop sign was blown through by the driver.
entries.see also: blow off, burn through, blow in

entries.meaning: To explode or destroy with explosives, to inflate, to lose your temper, to enlarge a picture, or to become famous overnight.
examples: The transformer blew up around two in the morning.
They blew the old span up on a Sunday.
Blow it up and start over.
Can you blow up the air mattress?
He blew the balloons up while the kids napped.
She blew up at the contractor.
He blows up over nothing and apologizes an hour later.
Blow the frame up and you can read the plate.
The song blew up over one weekend.
A minor complaint blew up into a lawsuit.

senses.head: Explode, or destroy with explosives
body: Both directions: the thing explodes, or somebody explodes it. (взорваться, взорвать)
examples: The transformer blew up around two in the morning.
They blew the old span up on a Sunday.
Blow it up and start over.

senses.head: Inflate
body: Of balloons, mattresses, and tires. (надуть)
examples: Can you blow up the air mattress?
He blew the balloons up while the kids napped.

senses.head: Lose your temper
body: Informal, often blow up at someone. (вспылить, взорваться)
examples: She blew up at the contractor.
He blows up over nothing and apologizes an hour later.

senses.head: Enlarge a picture
body: Of photographs and scans; the noun is a blowup. (увеличить)
examples: Blow the frame up and you can read the plate.

senses.head: Become suddenly popular
body: Informal and recent, of songs, videos, and people. (взлететь, выстрелить)
examples: The song blew up over one weekend.

senses.head: Get out of hand
body: Of a small problem that swells. (раздуться, разрастись)
examples: A minor complaint blew up into a lawsuit.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: взорвать(ся); надуть; вспылить; увеличить (снимок); резко прославиться
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — blow up the bridge or blow the bridge up, and a pronoun must split: blow it up, never ✗ blow up it. Senses 3, 5, and 6 take no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, whether the thing explodes on its own (sense 1, intransitive) or somebody explodes it (sense 1, transitive). Senses 3, 5, and 6 — losing your temper, becoming famous, getting out of hand — are dynamic intransitives; none of the senses is stative or linking.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the old span was blown up on a Sunday, the air mattress had already been blown up, blow the frame up → the frame was blown up until you could read the plate. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ the transformer was blown up at two in the morning (in the 'it exploded' reading), ✗ the song was blown up over one weekend.
entries.see also: blow out, blow away, blow off, burst out

entries.meaning: To pull free of a grip, to split off from a group or a tradition, or to pull ahead of the pack.
examples: He broke away and ran for the door.
She broke away from the crowd at the gate.
Three counties tried to break away in 1861.
A dozen members broke away to form their own local.
Two riders broke away on the climb.

senses.head: Pull free
body: Of a person getting loose. (вырваться, высвободиться)
examples: He broke away and ran for the door.
She broke away from the crowd at the gate.

senses.head: Split off from a group
body: Of factions, unions, and regions. (отколоться, выйти из состава)
examples: Three counties tried to break away in 1861.
A dozen members broke away to form their own local.

senses.head: Pull ahead in a race
body: Of cyclists and runners; the noun is a breakaway. (оторваться)
examples: Two riders broke away on the climb.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: вырваться; отколоться, выйти из состава; оторваться (в гонке)
entries.separable: not applicable — break away takes no object; whatever you are leaving follows from. ✗ break the group away.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: pulling free, splitting off, and pulling ahead in a race. No stative or linking use; the noun breakaway comes from sense 3.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in every sense, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the crowd was broken away from, ✗ the union was broken away from by a dozen members. What you leave rides on from, and that phrase does not passivize.
entries.see also: break off, break out, break up, break with

entries.meaning: To stop working, to lose emotional control, to separate something into parts, or to decompose.
examples: The van broke down outside Amarillo.
Two elevators have broken down this month.
She broke down on the stand.
He broke down when they read the verdict.
Let's break down the estimate line by line.
Can you break the numbers down by region?
Break it down for me one more time.
Plastic like that never really breaks down.
Negotiations broke down after two days.
Firefighters broke down the door.

senses.head: Stop working
body: Of vehicles and machinery; the noun is a breakdown. (сломаться, заглохнуть)
examples: The van broke down outside Amarillo.
Two elevators have broken down this month.

senses.head: Collapse emotionally
body: Of a person who cannot hold it together. (разрыдаться, сорваться)
examples: She broke down on the stand.
He broke down when they read the verdict.

senses.head: Separate into parts, itemize
body: Of costs, data, and arguments — the sense that splits most freely. (разбить на части, разложить)
examples: Let's break down the estimate line by line.
Can you break the numbers down by region?
Break it down for me one more time.

senses.head: Decompose
body: Of materials and chemicals. (разложиться, распасться)
examples: Plastic like that never really breaks down.

senses.head: Fail — of talks or a system
body: Of negotiations, order, and communication. (сорваться, зайти в тупик)
examples: Negotiations broke down after two days.

senses.head: Force open
body: Of a door under a battering ram or a shoulder. (выломать, вышибить)
examples: Firefighters broke down the door.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: сломаться; разрыдаться; разложить на части; разложиться; сорваться (о переговорах)
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — break down the costs or break the costs down, and a pronoun must split: break them down, never ✗ break down them. The stalled-car and crying senses take no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, both in the intransitive happenings (the van broke down, she broke down on the stand, negotiations broke down) and in the transitive acts (break down the estimate, break down the door). No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the numbers were broken down by region, the door was broken down by firefighters. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ the van was broken down outside Amarillo (that is the adjective, not the passive), ✗ negotiations were broken down after two days.
