entries.see also: break up, break in, break off, break through

entries.meaning: To take in exactly as much as you spend, so that you neither profit nor lose.
examples: The restaurant finally broke even in its third year.
We will break even on the trip if four more people sign up.
He sold the truck for what he paid and broke even.
The film has to gross twice its budget to break even.
They have not broken even since the second location opened.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on even, the word that completes the idiom
entries.separable: no — the phrase is frozen and nothing can come between the two words. ✗ break the business even.
entries.register: everyday — business vocabulary that everybody understands
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an achievement verb: reaching the point where income matches outlay. Even is a frozen resultative complement, so the phrase has the shape of a linking pattern (compare run dry, fall flat), but nothing may be substituted for it. The progressive is fine: we're breaking even this month.
entries.passive: no — the phrase takes no object at all, so there is nothing to make the subject: ✗ even was broken by the restaurant, ✗ the trip will be broken even on. The idea goes into the noun instead: the break-even point.
entries.see also: break down, buy out, bring in

entries.meaning: To enter a building illegally, to make new gear or a new person ready through use and training, or to interrupt.
examples: Someone broke in through the basement window.
They broke in twice in one summer.
It takes a season to break in a catcher's mitt.
Break the boots in before the hike.
Break them in slowly or you'll be sorry.
The anchor broke in with a bulletin.
Sorry to break in on your call.

senses.head: Enter illegally
body: No object here; the building follows into (see break into). The noun is a break-in. (вломиться, влезть)
examples: Someone broke in through the basement window.
They broke in twice in one summer.

senses.head: Wear in, train in
body: Of boots, gloves, engines, and new hires. (разносить, обкатать, приучить)
examples: It takes a season to break in a catcher's mitt.
Break the boots in before the hike.
Break them in slowly or you'll be sorry.

senses.head: Interrupt
body: Often break in on a conversation. (вмешаться, перебить)
examples: The anchor broke in with a bulletin.
Sorry to break in on your call.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes when it takes an object — break in a new glove or break the glove in, and a pronoun must split: break them in. The burglary and interrupting senses take no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense — forcing entry, wearing gear in, training a new hire, and interrupting. No stative or linking use; the noun is a break-in.
entries.passive: restricted — natural in the wear-in/train-in sense: the boots were broken in before the hike, new catchers are broken in slowly. The burglary sense is intransitive and has no passive (✗ the house was broken in — say broken into), and the interrupting sense passivizes only marginally: ?the call was broken in on.
entries.see also: break into, break out, break up, bust in

entries.meaning: To force your way into a place, to start something abruptly, or to get established in a field.
examples: Somebody broke into the shed and took the mower.
His car has been broken into twice this year.
The horse broke into a canter.
The whole section broke into applause.
He broke into a sweat just reading the number.
It took her ten years to break into television.
They are trying to break into the Mexican market.
We broke into the emergency water on day two.

senses.head: Force entry into
body: Of burglaries. (вломиться в, взломать)
examples: Somebody broke into the shed and took the mower.
His car has been broken into twice this year.

senses.head: Suddenly start
body: Of a run, a song, applause, tears, or a sweat. (вдруг начать, разразиться)
examples: The horse broke into a canter.
The whole section broke into applause.
He broke into a sweat just reading the number.

senses.head: Get established in a field or a market
body: Of an industry that is hard to enter. (пробиться, выйти на рынок)
examples: It took her ten years to break into television.
They are trying to break into the Mexican market.

senses.head: Open something kept for later
body: Of rations, savings, or a sealed pack. (начать, распечатать)
examples: We broke into the emergency water on day two.

entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.русский: вломиться в; вдруг начать, разразиться; пробиться (в отрасль)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ break the house into. Note that break it into pieces is a different, literal verb.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses, from forcing entry to suddenly starting a canter, a sweat, or applause. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1, where the prepositional passive is entirely ordinary — his car has been broken into twice this year, the shed was broken into over the weekend. The other senses do not passivize: ✗ a canter was broken into by the horse, ✗ television was broken into by her, ✗ the emergency water was broken into is at best marginal.
entries.see also: break in, break out, burst into, break through

entries.meaning: To snap a piece away, to end something abruptly, or to stop talking mid-sentence.
examples: Break off a piece and try it.
The handle broke off in my hand.
She broke a corner off and handed it to me.
The two sides broke off negotiations.
She broke off the engagement in April.
He broke it off by text, which tells you everything.
He broke off when he saw who had walked in.

senses.head: Snap away, detach
body: Of a piece coming off a whole, with or without an agent. (отломить, отломиться)
examples: Break off a piece and try it.
The handle broke off in my hand.
She broke a corner off and handed it to me.

senses.head: End abruptly
body: Of talks, engagements, and diplomatic relations. (прервать, разорвать)
examples: The two sides broke off negotiations.
She broke off the engagement in April.
He broke it off by text, which tells you everything.

senses.head: Stop speaking suddenly
body: Of a sentence left hanging. (оборвать себя, замолчать)
examples: He broke off when he saw who had walked in.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — break off a piece or break a piece off, and a pronoun must split: break it off, never ✗ break off it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, and sense 1 works both ways: somebody breaks a piece off, or the piece breaks off by itself. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — negotiations were broken off after two days, the engagement was broken off in April, a corner had been broken off. No passive when nothing does the breaking (✗ the handle was broken off in my hand in the intransitive reading — that is the adjective) or in the stop-speaking sense.
entries.see also: break down, break up, break away, break with

entries.meaning: To start suddenly (of fire, war, or fighting), to escape, to come out in a rash, or to bring something out for use.
examples: Fighting broke out near the border.
A fire broke out in the kitchen just after closing.
Two inmates broke out over the weekend.
He broke out in hives.
Her face breaks out whenever finals come around.
Break out the good glasses.
They broke the sparklers out at dusk.
Break them out — we're celebrating.
Can you break out the costs by department?

senses.head: Start suddenly
body: Of fires, fights, epidemics, and wars; the noun is an outbreak. (вспыхнуть, разразиться)
examples: Fighting broke out near the border.
A fire broke out in the kitchen just after closing.

senses.head: Escape
body: Of prisoners; the place escaped from follows of (see break out of). (сбежать, вырваться)
examples: Two inmates broke out over the weekend.

senses.head: Come out in a rash
body: Always break out in hives, spots, or a sweat. (покрыться сыпью, высыпать)
examples: He broke out in hives.
Her face breaks out whenever finals come around.

senses.head: Bring out for use
body: Informal, of something saved for an occasion. (достать, выставить)
examples: Break out the good glasses.
They broke the sparklers out at dusk.
Break them out — we're celebrating.

senses.head: Separate data into categories
body: Business usage; the noun is a breakout. (разбить, детализировать)
examples: Can you break out the costs by department?

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: вспыхнуть (о войне, пожаре); сбежать; высыпать (о сыпи); достать (припасённое)
entries.separable: yes in senses 4 and 5 — break out the good glasses or break the good glasses out, and a pronoun must split: break them out. The other senses take no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: fires and fights start (sense 1), prisoners escape (sense 2), a rash appears (sense 3), and somebody produces the good glasses (sense 4) or itemizes the costs (sense 5). No stative or linking use; the nouns are an outbreak and a breakout.
entries.passive: restricted — fine in the two transitive senses: the sparklers were broken out at dusk, the costs were broken out by department. No passive of senses 1–3, which take no object: ✗ a fire was broken out in the kitchen, ✗ hives were broken out in by him.
entries.see also: break out of, break in, break up, burst out

entries.meaning: To escape from a place, or to get free of a pattern you are stuck in.
examples: Three men broke out of the county jail in 1974.
Two accomplices broke him out of a federal facility.
The team can't break out of this slump.
She broke out of the habit by changing her commute.
Sales finally broke out of the range they had been stuck in.

senses.head: Escape from a place
body: Of jails and camps. (сбежать из, вырваться из)
examples: Three men broke out of the county jail in 1974.
Two accomplices broke him out of a federal facility.

senses.head: Get free of a pattern
body: Of slumps, habits, ruts, and trading ranges. (вырваться из, выйти из)
examples: The team can't break out of this slump.
She broke out of the habit by changing her commute.
Sales finally broke out of the range they had been stuck in.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on out, the first of the two particles
entries.русский: сбежать из; вырваться из (рутины, полосы неудач)
entries.separable: no when the subject is the one escaping — broke out of jail, ✗ broke jail out of. A separate pattern, break somebody out of somewhere, puts the person you are freeing right after the verb: they broke him out of jail.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, escaping a place and escaping a pattern. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — only the break somebody out of somewhere pattern passivizes: he was broken out of a federal facility by two accomplices. The ordinary escape and pattern senses do not: ✗ the county jail was broken out of, ✗ the slump can't be broken out of.
entries.see also: break out, break away, break through, bust out

entries.meaning: To force a way through a barrier, or to make a decisive advance.
examples: Protesters broke through the barricade.
The sun finally broke through around noon.
The lab broke through on the third try.
She broke through with her fourth novel.
Nothing I said broke through.

senses.head: Force a way through
body: Of crowds, lines, ice, and cloud. (пробиться, прорваться)
examples: Protesters broke through the barricade.
The sun finally broke through around noon.

senses.head: Make a decisive advance
body: Of research and careers; the noun is a breakthrough. (совершить прорыв)
examples: The lab broke through on the third try.
She broke through with her fourth novel.

senses.head: Get past somebody's resistance
body: Of an attempt to reach a person emotionally. (достучаться)
examples: Nothing I said broke through.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional verb when an object follows
entries.separable: no — whatever you break through follows the whole phrase: broke through the barricade, never ✗ broke the barricade through.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses, of forcing a way through a barrier, of a decisive advance, and of reaching somebody emotionally. No stative or linking use; the noun is a breakthrough.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is possible in sense 1 but stiff: the barricade was finally broken through; most writers keep the active. Senses 2 and 3 take no object and have no passive at all: ✗ the third try was broken through on.
entries.see also: break into, break out, break down

entries.meaning: To end a relationship, to disperse a crowd, to divide something into pieces, or — of a signal — to cut in and out.
examples: They broke up after four years.
She broke up with him over spring break.
Police broke up the crowd.
Break it up, you two.
He broke the fight up before anyone got hurt.
Break up the chocolate and fold it in.
They broke the estate up into six lots.
You're breaking up — say that again.
That impression breaks me up every time.
In England the schools break up next Friday; here they let out.

senses.head: End a romantic relationship
body: Often break up with somebody. (расстаться, разойтись)
examples: They broke up after four years.
She broke up with him over spring break.

senses.head: Disperse or separate
body: Of crowds, fights, and companies. (разогнать, разнять)
examples: Police broke up the crowd.
Break it up, you two.
He broke the fight up before anyone got hurt.

senses.head: Divide into pieces or parts
body: Of estates, blocks of ice, and chocolate. (разбить, раздробить)
examples: Break up the chocolate and fold it in.
They broke the estate up into six lots.

senses.head: Cut in and out — of a signal
body: Of a phone call losing reception. (пропадать, прерываться)
examples: You're breaking up — say that again.

senses.head: Make somebody laugh helplessly
body: Informal; the person goes in the middle. (рассмешить до слёз)
examples: That impression breaks me up every time.

senses.head: Begin vacation — British
body: Of schools. An American school lets out. (уходить на каникулы)
examples: In England the schools break up next Friday; here they let out.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: расстаться, разойтись; разогнать, разнять; разбить на части; пропадать (о связи)
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — break up the fight or break the fight up, and a pronoun must split: break it up, never ✗ break up it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from ending a relationship to dispersing a crowd to a signal cutting in and out. No stative or linking use; note that broken up in he was pretty broken up about it is an adjective (upset), not this passive.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the crowd was broken up by police, the estate was broken up into six lots, the fight was broken up before anyone got hurt. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ they were broken up after four years in the relationship reading, ✗ you were broken up on the call.
entries.see also: break down, break off, break away, bust up

entries.meaning: To end your association with a person, a party, or a long-standing practice.
examples: The governor broke with his own party on the vote.
The design breaks with a century of practice.
She broke with the family firm in 2011 and never went back.
Few candidates are willing to break with the base.
It was the first budget to break with the old formula.
entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ break tradition with, ✗ break it with.
entries.register: formal — commonest in writing about politics, family, and tradition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: an act of ending an association, not a state of being apart. No stative or linking use; the progressive is fine (he is breaking with the party on this).
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is grammatical but stilted, and formal writing tends to recast: ?a century of practice was broken with, ?the old formula had been broken with. The active is the normal form: the design breaks with a century of practice.
entries.see also: break off, break away, break up

entries.meaning: To make something happen.
examples: The strike brought about the first real contract in a decade.
Nothing brought about the change faster than the lawsuit.
What brought this about?
Two people brought it about, and neither got any credit.
The reforms were brought about by pressure from below.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — bring about a change or bring a change about, though the unsplit order is far commoner; with a pronoun it must split: bring it about, never ✗ bring about it.
entries.register: formal — commoner in writing than in speech, where Americans say cause
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and causative: making something happen. No stative or linking use, though it takes abstract subjects freely (the strike brought about the contract).
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is one of its commonest shapes in formal writing — the reforms were brought about by pressure from below, the change was brought about faster by the lawsuit than by anything else.
entries.see also: bring on, bring down, bring off

entries.meaning: To take somebody or something with you; also, to help somebody or something develop.
examples: Bring along a jacket — it gets cold on the water.
She brought her sister along.
Bring him along; there's room in the truck.
The staff is bringing the rookie along slowly.
Warm weather brought the tomatoes along fast.

senses.head: Take with you
body: Of people and gear. (взять с собой, прихватить)
examples: Bring along a jacket — it gets cold on the water.
She brought her sister along.
Bring him along; there's room in the truck.

senses.head: Help develop
body: Of rookies, students, and crops. (натаскивать, помогать расти)
examples: The staff is bringing the rookie along slowly.
Warm weather brought the tomatoes along fast.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: взять с собой, прихватить; помочь развиться
entries.separable: yes — bring along a friend or bring a friend along, and a pronoun must split: bring her along, never ✗ bring along her.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: carrying somebody or something with you, and developing a rookie or a crop. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — natural in the develop sense: the rookie is being brought along slowly, the tomatoes were brought along by the warm weather. Grammatical but uncommon in sense 1, where the active or an imperative is normal: ?a jacket should be brought along.
entries.see also: bring back, bring in, bring up

entries.meaning: To revive somebody who has fainted, or to talk somebody into agreeing with you.
examples: Smelling salts brought him around.
It took two minutes to bring her around.
Give me an hour with the committee and I'll bring them around.
Nothing brought him around until he saw the numbers.
I'll bring the trailer around at eight.

senses.head: Revive from unconsciousness
body: Of somebody who has fainted. (привести в чувство)
examples: Smelling salts brought him around.
It took two minutes to bring her around.

senses.head: Win somebody over
body: Of an argument that eventually lands. (переубедить, склонить)
examples: Give me an hour with the committee and I'll bring them around.
Nothing brought him around until he saw the numbers.

senses.head: Bring something over to a place
body: Of a vehicle or a dish delivered. (подогнать, занести)
examples: I'll bring the trailer around at eight.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: привести в чувство; переубедить, склонить на свою сторону
entries.separable: yes — bring around the skeptics or bring the skeptics around, and with a person as the object it is almost always split: bring him around, never ✗ bring around him.
entries.register: everyday — bring round is the British form
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — reviving somebody, winning somebody over, and delivering something to a place. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes — he was brought around with smelling salts, the committee was brought around once they saw the numbers, the trailer was brought around at eight.
entries.see also: bring to, bring back, bring off

entries.meaning: To return something, to reinstate something that was gone, or to make somebody remember.
examples: Bring back my drill when you're done with it.
She brought the wrong size back twice.
Bring it back by Friday.
Two states voted to bring back the tax.
They brought the old logo back after the backlash.
That smell brings back my grandmother's kitchen.
The photos brought it all back.

senses.head: Return an item or a person
body: Of anything borrowed or taken away. (вернуть, привезти обратно)
examples: Bring back my drill when you're done with it.
She brought the wrong size back twice.
Bring it back by Friday.

senses.head: Reinstate, revive
body: Of laws, logos, shows, and traditions. (восстановить, вернуть)
examples: Two states voted to bring back the tax.
They brought the old logo back after the backlash.

senses.head: Make somebody remember
body: Of smells, songs, and photographs. (напомнить, навеять)
examples: That smell brings back my grandmother's kitchen.
The photos brought it all back.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — bring back the receipts or bring the receipts back, and a pronoun must split: bring them back, never ✗ bring back them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: returning a thing, reinstating a practice, and triggering a memory. No stative or linking use; the memory sense takes an inanimate subject (that smell brings back my grandmother's kitchen) but is still dynamic.
entries.passive: yes in senses 1 and 2 — the drill was never brought back, the tax was brought back by two states, the old logo was brought back after the backlash. The memory sense passivizes stiffly: ?it was all brought back by the photos; the active is normal.
entries.see also: bring up, bring out, bring in

entries.meaning: To cause something to fall, to reduce a number, or to make somebody unhappy.
examples: One reporter brought the mayor down.
Ground fire brought the helicopter down.
The scandal brought down three executives in a week.
The Fed is trying to bring down inflation.
Bring the heat down to a simmer.
Don't let one bad review bring you down.
The whole conversation brought me down.

senses.head: Cause to fall or collapse
body: Of governments, executives, aircraft, and game. (свалить, сбить, свергнуть)
examples: One reporter brought the mayor down.
Ground fire brought the helicopter down.
The scandal brought down three executives in a week.

senses.head: Reduce
body: Of prices, fever, heat, and inflation. (снизить, сбить)
examples: The Fed is trying to bring down inflation.
Bring the heat down to a simmer.

senses.head: Depress somebody
body: Informal; the person goes in the middle. (расстроить, испортить настроение)
examples: Don't let one bad review bring you down.
The whole conversation brought me down.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: свалить, свергнуть; снизить, сбить; расстроить, испортить настроение
entries.separable: yes — bring down the government or bring the government down, and a pronoun must split: bring it down, never ✗ bring down it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and causative in all three senses: toppling something, reducing a number, and depressing somebody. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes — the mayor was brought down by one reporter, the helicopter was brought down by ground fire, inflation has to be brought down. Sense 3 works too, usually with get: don't get brought down by one bad review.
entries.see also: bring up, bring in, bring about

entries.meaning: To move an event to an earlier date, to put an idea up for discussion, or to carry a figure over in accounting.
examples: They brought forward the hearing by two weeks.
Can we bring the deadline forward to the fifteenth?
No one brought it forward until the agenda was almost done.
The senator brought forward an amendment nobody had read.
The balance brought forward from last quarter was wrong.

senses.head: Move to an earlier date
body: Of hearings, deadlines, and meetings. (перенести на более ранний срок)
examples: They brought forward the hearing by two weeks.
Can we bring the deadline forward to the fifteenth?
No one brought it forward until the agenda was almost done.

senses.head: Put up for discussion
body: Of motions, amendments, and proposals. (выдвинуть, внести)
examples: The senator brought forward an amendment nobody had read.

senses.head: Carry over a figure
body: Bookkeeping usage. (перенести — сумму)
examples: The balance brought forward from last quarter was wrong.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: перенести на более ранний срок; выдвинуть (предложение); перенести (сумму)
entries.separable: yes — bring forward the hearing or bring the hearing forward, and a pronoun must split: bring it forward.
entries.register: formal — for the scheduling sense Americans usually say move up
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: rescheduling earlier, proposing, and carrying a figure over. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual form in the scheduling and bookkeeping senses — the hearing was brought forward by two weeks, an amendment nobody had read was brought forward, the balance brought forward from last quarter.
entries.see also: bring up, bring in, bring about

entries.meaning: To introduce a rule or a person into a situation, to earn money, or — of a jury — to return a verdict.
examples: The city brought in a curfew after the second fire.
They brought the new policy in over the summer.
The shop brings in about nine thousand a month.
Streaming brought it in, not ticket sales.
They brought in a consultant nobody had asked for.
Police brought him in for questioning.
The jury brought in a verdict of not guilty.

senses.head: Introduce a law, rule, or system
body: Of policies put into effect. (ввести, принять)
examples: The city brought in a curfew after the second fire.
They brought the new policy in over the summer.

senses.head: Earn, generate
body: Of revenue and takings. (приносить, зарабатывать)
examples: The shop brings in about nine thousand a month.
Streaming brought it in, not ticket sales.

senses.head: Call in for help or questioning
body: Of consultants, specialists, and suspects. (привлечь, доставить)
examples: They brought in a consultant nobody had asked for.
Police brought him in for questioning.

senses.head: Return a verdict
body: Courtroom usage. (вынести — о вердикте)
examples: The jury brought in a verdict of not guilty.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — bring in an expert or bring an expert in, and a pronoun must split: bring her in, never ✗ bring in her.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: introducing a rule, earning money, summoning somebody, and returning a verdict. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in senses 1, 3, and 4 — a curfew was brought in after the second fire, he was brought in for questioning, a verdict of not guilty was brought in. The earning sense resists it, as measure-like objects usually do: ✗ nine thousand a month is brought in by the shop.
entries.see also: bring on, bring out, bring up, buy in

entries.meaning: To succeed at something difficult.
examples: Nobody thought they could bring off a live broadcast from the site.
She brought it off with an hour to spare.
It's a hard trick, and he brought it off twice in one night.
The team brought off the upset on the road.
If anyone can bring this off, she can.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — bring off a rescue or bring the rescue off, and a pronoun must split: bring it off, never ✗ bring off it.
entries.register: everyday — pull off is commoner in American speech
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: succeeding at something difficult, an achievement verb. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical (the upset was brought off on the road, a live broadcast from the site had never been brought off before) but the active dominates, and American speech reaches for pulled off instead.
entries.see also: bring about, bring in, break even

entries.meaning: To cause something (usually unwelcome) to start, or to add somebody to a team.
examples: Stress brought on the migraine.
Cold air brings it on every winter.
What brought this on?
They brought on two more engineers in March.
We brought her on as a contractor first.
You want a rematch? Bring it on.

senses.head: Cause, trigger
body: Of attacks, illnesses, and moods. (вызвать, спровоцировать)
examples: Stress brought on the migraine.
Cold air brings it on every winter.
What brought this on?

senses.head: Hire, add to a roster
body: Business usage; somebody brought on in March is onboarded in March. (взять, привлечь)
examples: They brought on two more engineers in March.
We brought her on as a contractor first.

senses.head: Bring it on — a challenge
body: Informal, and frozen with it. (давай, поглядим)
examples: You want a rematch? Bring it on.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: вызвать, спровоцировать; взять (в команду); давай, начинай
entries.separable: yes — bring on a migraine or bring a migraine on, and a pronoun must split: bring it on, never ✗ bring on it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: triggering something, hiring somebody, and the frozen challenge bring it on. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in senses 1 and 2 — the migraine was brought on by stress, two more engineers were brought on in March, she was brought on as a contractor first. The challenge is frozen with it and has no passive: ✗ it was brought on.
entries.see also: bring in, bring about, bring out

entries.meaning: To release a product, to make a quality show, or to draw something out of a person.
examples: They bring out a new edition every fall.
The label brought it out on vinyl first.
Salt brings out the sweetness.
That blue brings her eyes out.
Pressure brings out the best in some people and the worst in others.
Bring out the folding chairs before it gets dark.

senses.head: Release, publish
body: Of books, records, and models. (выпустить, издать)
examples: They bring out a new edition every fall.
The label brought it out on vinyl first.

senses.head: Make a quality more noticeable
body: Of salt, light, and color. (подчеркнуть, выявить)
examples: Salt brings out the sweetness.
That blue brings her eyes out.

senses.head: Draw something out of a person
body: Of pressure, kindness, or a crisis. (раскрыть, пробудить)
examples: Pressure brings out the best in some people and the worst in others.

senses.head: Produce something for use
body: Of chairs, files, and food carried out. (вынести, достать)
examples: Bring out the folding chairs before it gets dark.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: выпустить (в продажу); подчеркнуть, выявить; раскрыть (в человеке)
entries.separable: yes — bring out a new model or bring the new model out, and a pronoun must split: bring it out, never ✗ bring out it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: releasing a product, making a quality noticeable, drawing something out of a person, and carrying something out for use. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes — a new edition is brought out every fall, it was brought out on vinyl first, the folding chairs were brought out before dark. Sense 2 passivizes but sounds stiff: ?the sweetness is brought out by salt.
entries.see also: bring in, bring up, bear out, bring back

entries.meaning: To bring somebody back to consciousness.
examples: Cold water brought him to.
It took a minute to bring her to.
The medics brought the driver to at the scene.
Nothing would bring him to until the ambulance arrived.
She fainted in the hallway, and a neighbor brought her to.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on to, which here is an adverb and keeps its full vowel
entries.русский: привести в чувство, привести в сознание
entries.separable: yes, and obligatorily — the object sits in the middle: bring her to, bring the patient to. ✗ bring to her, which would mean something else entirely.
entries.register: everyday — slightly old-fashioned; a paramedic says revive
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: restoring somebody to consciousness, an achievement verb with a fixed adverbial to. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — the passive exists (she was brought to by cold water, the driver was brought to at the scene) but is uncommon; because the object must sit in the middle in the active, the passive strands to and sounds stilted to many speakers, who say was revived instead.
entries.see also: bring around, bring back, bring down

entries.meaning: To raise a child, to mention a topic, to display something on a screen, or to vomit.
examples: She was brought up by her grandparents.
They brought three kids up on one salary.
Don't bring up the divorce tonight.
He brought it up twice at dinner.
Bring up the invoice and check the date.
Bring it up on the big monitor.
The baby brought up most of the bottle.

senses.head: Raise a child
body: Usually in the passive when it is about your own childhood. (воспитать, вырастить)
examples: She was brought up by her grandparents.
They brought three kids up on one salary.

senses.head: Mention, raise a subject
body: The commonest sense by far. (поднять, затронуть)
examples: Don't bring up the divorce tonight.
He brought it up twice at dinner.

senses.head: Display on a screen
body: Office and technical usage. (вывести, открыть)
examples: Bring up the invoice and check the date.
Bring it up on the big monitor.

senses.head: Vomit
body: Of a baby or a patient. (вырвать, стошнить)
examples: The baby brought up most of the bottle.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: воспитать, вырастить; поднять (тему); вывести на экран; вырвать
entries.separable: yes — bring up the subject or bring the subject up, and a pronoun must split: bring it up, never ✗ bring up it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: raising a child, mentioning a subject, displaying something on screen, and vomiting. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes, and sense 1 lives mainly in the passive — she was brought up by her grandparents, he was brought up on a farm. Also the divorce was brought up twice at dinner, the invoice was brought up on the big monitor.
entries.see also: bring back, bring out, bring down, break up

entries.meaning: To make something a permanent part of a plan, a contract, or a structure from the start.
examples: Build in an extra week for permits.
The contract builds in a penalty for late delivery.
They built a two-percent raise in from the first year.
If you need slack in the schedule, build it in now.
The shelves are built in, so they stay with the house.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — build in a margin or build a margin in, and a pronoun must split: build it in, never ✗ build in it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: making something a permanent part of a plan or a structure from the start. No stative or linking use, though the participle shades into an adjective (built-in shelves).
entries.passive: yes, and it is very common — a penalty for late delivery is built in, the shelves are built in, so they stay with the house, a two-percent raise was built in from the first year.
entries.see also: build into, build up, build on

entries.meaning: To make something a permanent part of a larger thing, named after into.
examples: They built a review step into the process.
Build some slack into the schedule.
The penalty is built into the lease.
We built redundancy into the system after the outage.
Somebody had built an error into the formula years earlier.
The fee isn't extra — we built it into the price.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: встроить во что-то, заложить во что-то
entries.separable: the object has no choice — it comes between the verb and into: build flexibility into the contract, build it into the schedule. ✗ build into the contract flexibility.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: making something a permanent part of a named larger thing. No stative or linking use; the resulting participle behaves adjectivally (the fee is built into the price).
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the commonest form — the penalty is built into the lease, redundancy was built into the system after the outage, an error had been built into the formula years earlier.
entries.see also: build in, build on, build up

entries.meaning: To use something as a foundation for further work, or to add a structure onto a building.
examples: The second album builds on the first.
We want to build on what the last team learned.
A career built on one lucky year is a short career.
They built on a mudroom.
He built a screened porch on last spring.
The porch isn't original — they built it on in the eighties.

senses.head: Use as a foundation
body: Of research, success, and earlier work. Inseparable. (опираться на, развивать)
examples: The second album builds on the first.
We want to build on what the last team learned.
A career built on one lucky year is a short career.

senses.head: Add an extension
body: Of construction, where on is an adverb and moves freely. (пристроить)
examples: They built on a mudroom.
He built a screened porch on last spring.
The porch isn't original — they built it on in the eighties.

entries.pronunciation note: in sense 1 the verb keeps the stress (BUILD on it); in sense 2, where on is an adverb, the particle takes it (built a porch ON)
entries.type: prepositional verb (verb + preposition) in sense 1; phrasal verb in sense 2
entries.separable: no in sense 1 — build on last year's success, ✗ build last year's success on. In sense 2, where on means 'as an addition', it does split, and a pronoun must split: build on a porch, build a porch on, build it on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: using something as a foundation, and adding a structure to a building. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — sense 1 passivizes freely as a participle (a career built on one lucky year, the method was built on what the last team learned), but a full agentive passive is awkward: ?the first album was built on by the second. Sense 2 is fine: the porch was built on in the eighties.
entries.see also: build up, build in, bear out

entries.meaning: To accumulate gradually, to strengthen something over time, or to talk something up in advance.
examples: Sediment builds up behind the dam.
Pressure had been building up for months.
She is building up her mileage before the race.
Two years of therapy built his confidence up.
Build it up slowly — a mile a week.
They built the sequel up so much that it couldn't win.
Don't build it up too much or she'll be disappointed.

senses.head: Accumulate
body: Of sediment, pressure, plaque, and resentment; the noun is a buildup. (накапливаться, скапливаться)
examples: Sediment builds up behind the dam.
Pressure had been building up for months.

senses.head: Increase or strengthen something
body: Of mileage, muscle, confidence, and savings. (наращивать, укреплять)
examples: She is building up her mileage before the race.
Two years of therapy built his confidence up.
Build it up slowly — a mile a week.

senses.head: Praise in advance, hype
body: Of sequels, candidates, and blind dates. (расхваливать, раздувать)
examples: They built the sequel up so much that it couldn't win.
Don't build it up too much or she'll be disappointed.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — build up your strength or build your strength up, and a pronoun must split: build it up. The accumulating sense takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: accumulating, strengthening, and hyping. No stative or linking use; the noun is a buildup and built-up is a separate adjective.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — her mileage is being built up before the race, his confidence was built up over two years of therapy, the sequel was built up so much that it couldn't win. No passive of the accumulating sense: ✗ sediment is built up behind the dam by the river.
entries.see also: build in, build on, bring up

entries.meaning: To destroy a building by fire, or — of a building — to be destroyed by fire.
examples: Vandals burned down the old depot.
They burned the whole block down in one night.
The church burned down in 1908 and was never rebuilt.
Insurance won't help them if they burn it down on purpose.
Two barns have burned down on that road in five years.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — burn down the barn or burn the barn down, and a pronoun must split: burn it down, never ✗ burn down it. When the building is the subject there is no object at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and it works both ways: somebody burns the building down, or the building burns down by itself. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the old depot was burned down by vandals, the whole block was burned down in one night. No passive when the building is the subject: ✗ the church was burned down in 1908 is the causative reading only, not the intransitive one.
entries.see also: burn up, burn out, burn off

entries.meaning: To get rid of something by burning it or using it up; of fog, to clear as the day warms.
examples: A four-mile walk burns off about four hundred calories.
He burned the nervous energy off at the gym.
Crews burned off the underbrush before the dry season.
Burn it off rather than scrape it.
The fog usually burns off by ten.

senses.head: Use up energy or calories
body: Of exercise and nervous energy. (сжечь, израсходовать)
examples: A four-mile walk burns off about four hundred calories.
He burned the nervous energy off at the gym.

senses.head: Remove by burning
body: Of brush, paint, and stubble. (выжечь, выпалить)
examples: Crews burned off the underbrush before the dry season.
Burn it off rather than scrape it.

senses.head: Clear — of fog
body: Intransitive, and standard in coastal weather reports. (рассеяться)
examples: The fog usually burns off by ten.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — burn off the calories or burn the calories off, and a pronoun must split: burn them off. The fog sense takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: using up energy, removing something by burning, and fog clearing. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in senses 1 and 2 — the underbrush was burned off before the dry season, about four hundred calories are burned off on a four-mile walk, the paint was burned off rather than scraped. No passive of the fog sense, which takes no object: ✗ the fog is burned off by ten.
entries.see also: burn up, burn out, bleed off

entries.meaning: To fail from overheating, to exhaust yourself past usefulness, or — of a fire — to go out for lack of fuel.
examples: The starter burned out twice in one winter.
You'll burn the motor out running it dry.
He burned it out in a week.
Half the residents burn out before their third year.
She burned herself out covering two jobs.
The fire burned out on its own by dawn.
Four families were burned out of the building.

senses.head: Fail from heat or overuse
body: Of bulbs, motors, and circuits. (перегореть, сгореть)
examples: The starter burned out twice in one winter.
You'll burn the motor out running it dry.
He burned it out in a week.

senses.head: Exhaust somebody through overwork
body: Of people; the noun is burnout. (выгореть, вымотаться)
examples: Half the residents burn out before their third year.
She burned herself out covering two jobs.

senses.head: Go out for lack of fuel
body: Of a fire left alone. (догореть, потухнуть)
examples: The fire burned out on its own by dawn.

senses.head: Be forced from a home by fire
body: Almost always passive. (лишиться жилья из-за пожара)
examples: Four families were burned out of the building.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: перегореть; выгореть (о человеке); догореть; лишиться жилья из-за пожара
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — burn out the motor or burn the motor out, and a pronoun must split: burn it out, burn yourself out. Senses 1 and 3 are also used without an object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: failing from heat, exhausting somebody, a fire dying, and losing a home to fire. No stative or linking use; burned out as in he looks burned out is the adjective.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses, and sense 4 is almost only passive — four families were burned out of the building; also the motor was burned out in a week, and with get in the exhaustion sense: half the residents get burned out before their third year. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ the starter was burned out twice (as an event), ✗ the fire was burned out by dawn.
entries.see also: burn up, burn down, burn through

entries.meaning: To use something up fast, or to make a hole in something by burning.
examples: They burned through the seed money in nine months.
We burn through a case of these every week.
The ember burned through the tarp.
The acid burned through two layers of glove.
She burned through the whole season in a weekend.

senses.head: Use up quickly
body: Of money, supplies, and staff. (просадить, промотать)
examples: They burned through the seed money in nine months.
We burn through a case of these every week.

senses.head: Make a hole by burning
body: The literal sense. (прожечь)
examples: The ember burned through the tarp.
The acid burned through two layers of glove.

senses.head: Get through work fast
body: Of a task finished in a hurry. (пролететь, быстро одолеть)
examples: She burned through the whole season in a weekend.

entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ burn the cash through, ✗ burn it through.
entries.register: everyday — the money sense is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: using something up fast, making a hole, and racing through work. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — best in the literal sense, where it is common: the tarp had been burned through, two layers of glove were burned through. The money and work senses passivize awkwardly and are usually left active: ?the seed money was burned through in nine months.
entries.see also: blow through, burn up, burn out

entries.meaning: To destroy or be destroyed completely by fire, to make somebody very angry, or to be feverish.
examples: The satellite burned up on reentry.
He burned every letter up in the fireplace.
It burns me up that nobody called.
That attitude burns her up.
The kid is burning up — get the thermometer.
They burned up four hundred miles before lunch.

senses.head: Destroy completely by fire
body: Of anything consumed rather than merely scorched. (сжечь, сгореть)
examples: The satellite burned up on reentry.
He burned every letter up in the fireplace.

senses.head: Make somebody angry
body: Informal, and the object never moves out of the middle. (бесить, злить)
examples: It burns me up that nobody called.
That attitude burns her up.

senses.head: Be feverish
body: Always in the continuous. (гореть — о больном)
examples: The kid is burning up — get the thermometer.

senses.head: Cover ground fast
body: Informal, in burn up the road and burn up the miles. (нестись, глотать километры)
examples: They burned up four hundred miles before lunch.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: сгореть дотла; бесить, злить; гореть (о температуре)
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — burn up the letters or burn the letters up, and a pronoun must split: burn them up. In the anger sense the object always sits in the middle: it burns me up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense. The fever sense is dynamic but locked in the progressive (the kid is burning up, not ✗ the kid burns up in that reading); the anger sense takes an inanimate subject and a frozen middle object.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1 — every letter was burned up in the fireplace, the papers had all been burned up. No in the anger sense, where the object never leaves the middle: ✗ I was burned up by it that nobody called (I was burned up about it is the adjective). The reentry, fever, and distance uses are intransitive and have no passive.
entries.see also: burn down, burn out, burn off

entries.meaning: To enter a room suddenly and noisily, or to interrupt.
examples: She burst in without knocking.
Two officers burst in through the side door.
Sorry to burst in on your meeting.
He burst in halfway through the toast.
The kids burst in soaked and shouting.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — burst in takes no object; whatever you interrupt follows on. ✗ burst the door in in this sense.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: entering suddenly, or interrupting. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in both senses, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the room was burst in. Even the prepositional burst in on barely passivizes: ?our meeting was burst in on, which most speakers would recast.
entries.see also: burst into, burst out, break in, bust in

entries.meaning: To rush suddenly into a place, or to start something abruptly — tears, laughter, song, or flame.
examples: He burst into the office without knocking.
Agents burst into the apartment at dawn.
She burst into tears at the gate.
The whole table burst into laughter.
The engine burst into flames on the runway.

senses.head: Rush into a place
body: Of anyone entering without warning. (ворваться в)
examples: He burst into the office without knocking.
Agents burst into the apartment at dawn.

senses.head: Suddenly start crying, laughing, or singing
body: A short fixed list of nouns follows: tears, laughter, song, applause. (разразиться, расплакаться)
examples: She burst into tears at the gate.
The whole table burst into laughter.

senses.head: Catch fire suddenly
body: Always burst into flames. (вспыхнуть)
examples: The engine burst into flames on the runway.

entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ burst tears into, ✗ burst it into.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: rushing into a place, suddenly crying or laughing, and catching fire. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive fails across the board: ✗ the office was burst into, ✗ the apartment was burst into by agents. In senses 2 and 3 the noun after into is part of a frozen phrase (tears, laughter, flames) and can never become a subject: ✗ tears were burst into.
entries.see also: burst in, burst out, break into

entries.meaning: To start laughing or crying suddenly, to say something abruptly, or to rush out of a place.
examples: Everyone burst out laughing.
She burst out crying in the parking lot.
"That's a lie," he burst out.
Smoke burst out of the vents.
They burst out of the building before the alarm stopped.

senses.head: Burst out laughing or crying
body: The -ing form attaches straight to the particle. (разразиться смехом, расплакаться)
examples: Everyone burst out laughing.
She burst out crying in the parking lot.

senses.head: Say something suddenly
body: Of an outburst, usually quoted. (выпалить)
examples: "That's a lie," he burst out.

senses.head: Rush out
body: Of people or smoke leaving fast. (выскочить, вырваться)
examples: Smoke burst out of the vents.
They burst out of the building before the alarm stopped.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — nothing may come between the two words; with laughing or crying the -ing form follows directly. ✗ burst him out laughing.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: starting to laugh or cry, blurting something out, and rushing out of a place. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — intransitive throughout, with no object anywhere: ✗ laughing was burst out, ✗ the building was burst out of. Even the quoted-speech sense ("That's a lie," he burst out) has no object to promote.
entries.see also: burst into, burst in, break out, blow up

entries.meaning: To force your way into a place, or to barge into a conversation.
examples: Somebody busted in through the back door.
The cops busted in before he could flush anything.
Don't bust in while she's on the phone.
He busted in halfway through my sentence.
They busted in and found the place empty.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: not applicable — bust in takes no object. ✗ bust him in, which would mean punching him.
entries.register: informal — American; the plain form is break in
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: forcing your way in, or barging into a conversation. Informal American; no stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in both senses: ✗ the back door was busted in is a different, literal verb (busting a door), not this one, and ✗ the conversation was busted in on is not idiomatic.
entries.see also: bust out, bust up, break in

entries.meaning: To escape, to produce something for use, or — with laughing — to start suddenly.
examples: Two of them busted out of the county jail.
His brother busted him out a week later.
He busted out the karaoke machine at midnight.
Bust them out — nobody's saving them for later.
The whole room busted out laughing.

senses.head: Escape
body: Of prisoners, and of whoever springs them. (сбежать, вырваться)
examples: Two of them busted out of the county jail.
His brother busted him out a week later.

senses.head: Take out and use
body: Informal, of something saved for the right moment. (достать, вытащить)
examples: He busted out the karaoke machine at midnight.
Bust them out — nobody's saving them for later.

senses.head: Bust out laughing
body: Informal for burst out laughing. (расхохотаться)
examples: The whole room busted out laughing.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — bust out the good bourbon or bust the good bourbon out, and a pronoun must split: bust it out, never ✗ bust out it. In the escape sense the escaper is usually the subject and there is no object (they busted out), but you can bust somebody out, and then the person splits the pair: his brother busted him out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: escaping, producing something for use, and starting to laugh. Informal; no stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — fine in the transitive senses: the karaoke machine was busted out at midnight, he was busted out of a federal facility a week later. No passive when the escaper is the subject or in the laughing sense: ✗ the county jail was busted out of, ✗ laughing was busted out.
entries.see also: bust up, bust in, break out

entries.meaning: To break up a fight or a gathering, to damage something badly, or — of a couple — to split.
examples: The bouncers busted up the fight.
Bust it up before somebody calls the cops.
He busted up the truck on a gravel road.
She busted her knee up skiing.
They busted up in the spring and nobody was surprised.

senses.head: Break up a fight or a party
body: Of bouncers and police. (разнять, разогнать)
examples: The bouncers busted up the fight.
Bust it up before somebody calls the cops.

senses.head: Damage, wreck
body: Of vehicles and body parts; the noun is a bust-up. (разбить, покорёжить)
examples: He busted up the truck on a gravel road.
She busted her knee up skiing.

senses.head: Split — of a couple
body: Informal for break up. (расстаться, разойтись)
examples: They busted up in the spring and nobody was surprised.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — bust up the fight or bust the fight up, and a pronoun must split: bust it up, never ✗ bust up it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: breaking up a fight, wrecking something, and a couple splitting. Informal; no stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in senses 1 and 2, and the informal get-passive is the natural form — the fight was busted up by the bouncers, the truck got busted up on a gravel road, her knee got busted up skiing. No passive of the couple sense: ✗ they were busted up in the spring.
entries.see also: bust out, bust in, break up

entries.meaning: To purchase something you or your company previously sold.
examples: The company bought back four million shares.
He sold the ring and bought it back a year later.
The dealer will buy the lease back if the mileage is low.
They bought them back for half what they got.
The town has been buying back land along the river.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — buy back the shares or buy the shares back, and a pronoun must split: buy them back, never ✗ buy back them.
entries.register: everyday — common in business writing, where the noun is a buyback
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: repurchasing what you sold. No stative or linking use; the noun is a buyback.
entries.passive: yes, and it is standard in business writing — four million shares were bought back last quarter, the ring was bought back a year later, the lease can be bought back if the mileage is low.
entries.see also: buy out, buy up, buy off

entries.meaning: To purchase a stake in something, or to accept an idea and get behind it.
examples: Two partners bought in before the second location opened.
If the staff doesn't buy in, the policy dies on paper.
He bought in early and sold at the top.
Nobody had bought in yet, so the plan stalled.
Management wants everyone to buy in by Friday.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: войти в долю, вложиться; принять идею, поддержать
entries.separable: not applicable — buy in takes no object; what you buy into follows into (see buy into). ✗ buy the plan in.
entries.register: everyday — the agreement sense is office vocabulary, and the noun buy-in is commoner than the verb
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: purchasing a stake, and getting behind an idea. No stative or linking use — even the agreement sense describes coming around, not being in a state.
entries.passive: no — it takes no object at all, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the plan was bought in, ✗ the policy hasn't been bought in yet. English puts the idea in the noun instead: we need staff buy-in.
entries.see also: buy into, buy out, buy up

entries.meaning: To accept an idea, often too readily; or to purchase a share of a business.
examples: I never bought into the whole story.
Half the country bought into it for about a year.
You don't have to buy into the theory to use the method.
She bought into the practice in 2016.
Two associates bought into the firm the year it expanded.

senses.head: Accept or believe an idea
body: Usually with a hint that the idea was oversold. (поверить в, купиться на)
examples: I never bought into the whole story.
Half the country bought into it for about a year.
You don't have to buy into the theory to use the method.

senses.head: Purchase a stake
body: Of practices, franchises, and funds. (войти в долю, купить долю)
examples: She bought into the practice in 2016.
Two associates bought into the firm the year it expanded.

entries.pronunciation note: a prepositional verb, so the stress stays on the verb and the preposition leans on it
entries.русский: поверить в, купиться на; войти в долю
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the preposition. ✗ buy the story into, ✗ buy it into.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: accepting an idea and purchasing a stake. No stative or linking use, though sense 1 often appears in the perfect describing a settled belief (he has bought into the theory).
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is marginal and mostly avoided: ?the theory has been widely bought into, ✗ the whole story was never bought into by me. The stake sense does not passivize at all: ✗ the practice was bought into in 2016.
entries.see also: buy in, buy out, bet on

entries.meaning: To pay somebody to stop opposing you or to keep quiet.
examples: They tried to buy off the two holdouts.
Somebody bought the inspector off.
You can't buy him off — he doesn't want money.
The witnesses were bought off long before the trial.
He bought them off with a consulting contract.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — buy off the inspector or buy the inspector off, and a pronoun must split: buy him off, never ✗ buy off him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: paying somebody to stop opposing you. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is common because the payer is often unknown — the witnesses were bought off long before the trial, the inspector had been bought off, they were bought off with a consulting contract.
entries.see also: buy out, buy up, buy back

entries.meaning: To purchase somebody's entire share of a business, or to pay to end a contract.
examples: His brother bought him out in 2019.
A private equity firm bought out the whole chain.
She bought her partner out over five years.
The club bought out the last year of his contract.
They offered to buy us out, and we said no.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.русский: выкупить долю; выкупить компанию; откупиться от контракта
entries.separable: yes — buy out the partner or buy the partner out, and a pronoun must split: buy him out, never ✗ buy out him.
entries.register: everyday — the noun is a buyout
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: purchasing somebody's whole share, or paying to end a contract. No stative or linking use; the noun is a buyout.
entries.passive: yes — he was bought out by his brother in 2019, the whole chain was bought out by a private equity firm, the last year of his contract was bought out.
entries.see also: buy in, buy back, buy up, buy off

entries.meaning: To purchase all or nearly all of something that is available.
examples: Investors bought up half the block in two years.
Somebody bought the whole print run up.
They bought it up before the zoning changed.
Shoppers had bought up every generator in the county.
The company is buying up its smaller competitors.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — buy up the land or buy the land up, and a pronoun must split: buy it up, never ✗ buy up it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: purchasing all of something available. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes — half the block was bought up in two years, every generator in the county had been bought up, the whole print run was bought up by one buyer.
entries.see also: buy out, buy back, buy in
